prompts.text:
# Live Countdown Split-screen — Style Prompt

> An edit style, not a look. Real footage of one event with a known zero (a launch, a verdict, a final whistle, polls closing), shown in real time: screen time equals event time, a clock ticks every second, and the screen splits into more and more cells as the moment nears, every cell showing the same second. At zero the cells merge into one picture and the clock flips.
> References (grammar only): the real-time clock and splitting screens of the TV series *24*; the multi-camera archive panels and mission-time codes of the documentary *Apollo 11* (2019). Never copy their type, colours, sounds, graphics or shots, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

1. **Real time.** One continuous stretch of the event, never cut, never re-ordered, never sped up. Slow-motion sources are played back at real speed. The clock and the picture can be checked against each other at any frame.
2. **The clock is the lead.** It ticks every whole second (sound and a falling digit), it says who is in control, and it changes state at zero.
3. **Cells show the same second.** Every video cell is synced to the clock, or says plainly that it is not (§8, "sync badge").
4. **The layout is the edit.** Cuts are layout changes, and every layout change lands on a real spoken call or event in the native sound, not on the music.
5. **More cells, closer to zero; one picture at zero.** The number of cells is the tension curve.

Not a montage (time jumps), not a security wall (the layout never moves), not a flashback structure (real time cannot go back), not a slide deck (cells that don't follow events, text filling the cells, centred titles with page turns).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Three kinds of material at once**: video cameras of the same moment (2–8), documents (a fact sheet, a filing, a schedule: shown as paper, never retyped as a slide), and photographs (the people of the day). Our own type explains them; type printed in the material is only picture.
- **Data drawn by us**: checklists, bars, a flight or process profile, a second countdown to the next milestone. Every number comes from an official source (§10).
- **Cells**: hard rectangles on near-black `#06080A`, 24 px outer margin, 8–9 px gutters, 1 px border `rgba(222,232,238,.16)`, a light radial vignette (to 36 % black) on video cells. No rounded corners, no drop shadows, no 3D.
- **Camera chip** top-left of every cell: dark plate 84 %, a square dot (orange = synced video, grey = unsynced or still), code (`CAM 4`, `DOC`, `LIST`), Chinese name, small English name.
- **Burned-in text in the sources** (broadcast bugs, camera IDs, timers, tracker readouts) is cropped by a per-shot usable region, or blurred out (ffmpeg `delogo`) after it has been used for syncing. Never shown as if it were ours.
- **One grade for every source** (ffmpeg): `eq=contrast=1.07:saturation=0.9:gamma=0.97:brightness=-0.01,colorbalance=rs=-0.02:bs=0.03:rh=0.03:bh=-0.02`, then film grain 1 at the master (`mux.sh … 1`). Cool shadows, slightly warm highlights: control rooms and launch pads look like one film.
- **Resolution**: modern footage at most 1.5× its source pixels; for a punch-in, extract that stretch at a higher resolution from the 4K source instead of enlarging a 1080p frame. Documents at ≥ 1 source pixel per screen pixel.

## 3. Colour logic

| Role | Value |
|---|---|
| Ground | `#06080A`; panels `#0B0E11` |
| Main text | `#F2F5F7`; secondary `#7C878D` |
| Accent: the T− sign, synced dots, ticks done, event flags, the active control segment | `#FF5B1F` |
| Speaking light, "heard" tags | `#FF3B30` |
| Plates over full-screen footage | `rgba(6,8,10,.80)` |
| After zero, the clock block | ground `#FF5B1F`, text `#0A0B0C` (inverted) |

Orange means "now / synced / done". Grey means "pending / not synced". Nothing else is coloured; colour belongs to the footage.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- Clock digits: a condensed sans with fixed-width digit slots (ours: Barlow Condensed SemiBold, drawn digit by digit in equal slots so the clock never jitters); size up to 132 px, the T−/T+ sign at 0.85×, tenths at 0.41× in grey, a ten-segment sub-second bar under it.
- Chinese: a sturdy sans (ours: Noto Sans SC 500/700, subset). English text: a clean grotesque (Barlow). Labels, codes and English small print: a monospace (IBM Plex Mono). All OFL, in the project's `fonts/`.
- **The live transcript is the subtitle.** A fixed box (bottom right, or a cell in the grid): a speaking light and the speaker type (commentary / loop / narrator — the narrator, our own voice, is marked in orange so it is never mistaken for the event's audio), the English line appearing word by word at the spoken times (0.08 s fade per word, a block cursor), the Chinese line whole when its cue starts. **One line per language, never wrapped**: a long sentence becomes two cues; each cue ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s). Transcribe only what is said; mark doubtful words in `FACTS.md`.
- Reading time for everything else: CJK ÷ 4.5 + other ÷ 15 + 1.5 s from the moment it is complete (`readcheck.mjs`). A comparison (two bars, two numbers) stays fully on screen ≥ 2.5 s.

## 5. Motion quality

- 30 fps. Clock: on each whole second the new digits drop 14 px in 0.12 s (ease-out); the sub-second bar empties one segment per 0.1 s (fills after zero).
- Re-layout: 0.34 s `easeInOutCubic`. Cells that stay interpolate their rectangles; new cells open from their left edge; leaving cells close to the left; a new cell flashes a 3 px orange border for ~0.2 s when it lands. A grid filling up pops one cell per spoken count in 0.30 s.
- Swaps (one source replaces another in the same rectangle) wipe in from the left. Hard cuts only between full-screen sources.
- Photographs push in ≤ 6 % over their whole stay; names pop one by one 0.16 s apart. Documents move their window down a row in 0.45 s; the highlight sweeps left to right in 0.35 s.
- Never: slow push-ins on video to fake motion, page-turn transitions, centred pop-up words, speed ramps.

## 6. Edit grammar

- **Screen time = event time.** One mapping, `M = t − T0`, for the whole film. Each camera has its own source offset (`s = M + c`) measured once and baked into the frame extraction (`demo/tools/prep.sh`): frames are named by film frame number, so the page never computes sync.
- **Cut points are calls.** Each layout change starts on the first word of a real call in the native audio ("ten", "go for…", "ignition", a name) or on an event visible in the footage. The music follows; it never sets a cut.
- **Cell count rises toward zero**: 1 → 2 → 3–4 → many (6–9, the clock itself becomes the centre cell, the transcript a cell) → **one** at zero → a few again after zero (the event's consequences) → one under the title. The shortest layouts are nearest to zero.
- **Inside a cell, the source cuts itself** (a broadcast switching cameras): keep it; we only cut the layout.
- **Silence before zero**: the music drops out a quarter-second before zero; only the native sound and the clock remain.
- Full-screen moments carry the clock and transcript as plates at the bottom; a gradient (0 → 75 % black) under them.

## 7. Sound palette

Layers, top to bottom:

1. **Native sound** — the event's own audio (commentary, radio loops, crowd), high-pass 90 Hz, compressed, always on top; never ducked.
2. **Narrator** (sparingly, only in gaps of the native sound, never over it): clean and close, a different gender or accent from the event's voices; Kokoro, every line through `asr_check.py`.
3. **The clock**: a tick every whole second (two alternating pitches around 1.5–1.9 kHz, panned ±15 %), louder in the last ten seconds, a soft single pitch after zero.
4. **Interface foley** from `window.EV`: re-layout whoosh + metallic snap; cell pop snap; checklist tock; event-flag whoosh; full-screen cut thump.
5. **Score**, 60 BPM so one beat = one second = one tick: a low synth drone whose low-pass opens toward zero, a bass drum per beat, off-beat hats, a tom per spoken count, timpani roll into zero, silence, then a low brass major chord with bass drum, crash and tubular bell at zero; after zero a new texture (pizzicato bass ostinato, lighter tick). Low brass, timpani, toms, tubular bells, glockenspiel; no piano-and-strings pad.
- Mix: music about 8–10 dB under the native sound and ducked under speech; the ignition (or the event's own climax sound) is the loudest moment; master −14 LUFS via a pre-limited mix so `mux.sh` meets the true-peak target.
- **Changing the music** (e.g. a Suno track): never move the clock or the cuts; choose or stretch a track so a downbeat lands exactly on zero and a section change lands on T−10, and keep the quarter-second silence before zero.

## 8. Native moves (and how to build them)

- **Many into one.** At zero, every cell moves to its tile of the full frame (a 3×3 grid becomes nine 640×360 tiles) while each tile cross-fades to the same full-screen shot, chips and borders vanish in the first half, a warm white flash (`rgba(255,248,236,.7)`, decay τ ≈ 0.11 s) peaks, and the clock and transcript slide from their grid cells back to the bottom. 0.42 s. *Fits:* a verdict read out; the goal at the final whistle.
- **Clock inversion.** At zero the clock block flips from dark with an orange T− to orange with dark T+, and its header changes (countdown → elapsed). *Fits:* polls closing, a store opening.
- **Control strip.** Segments in the clock header (who has control: ground → vehicle → mission control; prosecution → jury → judge); the active one fills orange on the call that hands it over, with a short flash. The story's turns live here.
- **The grid fills on the count.** Empty grid slots show as dashed "standby" frames; each spoken number opens one camera. *Fits:* "three, two, one" before a premiere.
- **Sync badge.** Top-right of each video cell: `● 实时同步 LIVE SYNC` (synced), `○ 同一时段 · 未逐帧同步 SAME WINDOW` (hatched, grey: footage from the same minutes without a usable clock), `慢动作还原 1× REAL-TIME` (slow-motion re-timed). Honesty is part of the look.
- **Planned vs heard checklist.** Official milestones with their planned times tick as the clock passes them; when the native audio actually says one, a red "heard −32.1" tag with a small waveform appears beside it. *Fits:* a court schedule against what was said; a train timetable against the platform announcement.
- **Second countdown.** After zero, a smaller clock counts to the next official milestone (`−1:47 to booster separation, expected T+2:09`) along a schematic profile drawn by time, not distance. *Fits:* the next race split; the next ballot count.
- **Event flag.** An orange bar with black type slides in at the bottom of the relevant cell on its call (`RS-25 ×4 启动 ENGINE START · T−6.36`), held ≥ the reading time.
- **Punch-in on a call.** A hard digital punch-in on the relevant detail when the commentary names it, from a higher-resolution extraction of the same source.
- **Document by rows.** A paper close-up shows two or three rows; a highlight bar and an annotation band below the paper translate the row; the window moves only between rows (its edges in the white space).

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Unsyncable footage** (an edited "rover" reel with no clock or event to align on). Never fake it: label the cell "same window · not frame-synced", keep it out of the countdown's key seconds or use it only where nothing it shows contradicts the time, and say so in `FACTS.md`. Look first for a source with a burned-in timer, a visible ignition / flash / whistle, or the same audio.
- **Measuring zero.** Never trust metadata. Combine two independent marks: a visible event (ignition flash, a broadcast countdown bug's flip) and the spoken word timing ("booster" at zero). Re-measure on the file you actually cut: `ffmpeg -ss … -c copy` starts on the previous keyframe.
- **Audio and picture of one file can disagree** (a switched feed whose audio lagged its video by ~1 s). Sync each camera on its picture.
- **Slow-motion sources**: measure the factor from two events with a known gap (e.g. engine start to booster ignition = 6.36 s) and re-time with `setpts=PTS/k`.
- **Burned-in text**: broadcast bugs, camera numbers, timers, tracker data. Define per-shot usable regions (they change when the source cuts) or `delogo` them; check every source cut with a frame-difference scan.
- **A static wide shot for ten seconds** reads as flat. Give every 1–2 seconds a new element (a cell, a tick on the list, a flag, a punch-in), not a fake camera move.
- **Spoilers in the subtitle**: a whole-sentence Chinese line reveals the end of a count early. Split counts into separate cues.
- **The clock jitters** if digits are proportional: draw them in fixed slots.
- **Hot peaks** from broadcast audio and the ignition hit miss the true-peak target: pre-limit the mix at about −4 dBFS after normalising to −14 LUFS.
- **Logos.** No agency insignia as a graphic; cut slates and bugs; the film says it is unofficial.

## 10. Materials, sources, facts, engine

**Materials — ask first.** Before searching, ask the user whether they have their own material of the event: footage from several angles, recordings of the audio, photos, documents (schedules, filings, results), data. What they give comes first and is credited as they say.

**If not, where to look** (each item's own page decides; record it):
- **NASA** (images.nasa.gov, svs.gsfc.nasa.gov): U.S. federal government works, public domain in the U.S.; fine to use. Don't use NASA insignia as graphics or imply endorsement; check each item for third-party material.
- **Other U.S. federal agencies** (NOAA, National Archives, DoD DVIDS): public domain, same check for third-party material.
- **Internet Archive**: only items whose own record shows public domain (pre-1931 U.S. publications, U.S. government works) or CC0 / CC BY; skip `youtube-*` / "mirrortube" uploads and anything of unclear origin.
- **Wikimedia Commons**: read each file page; CC0, public domain and CC BY are fine (credit CC BY in full); CC BY-SA and "no known restrictions" are not fine without the user's explicit agreement.
- **Library of Congress**: check each item's rights statement; "no known restrictions" is not CC0.
- Not usable: re-uploads without a source, restored or colourised versions, news-agency footage, anything whose licence is not stated.

**Before downloading, tell the user** what you will fetch, from where and under which licence, in one message. Then fetch only the seconds you need: `python3 demo/tools/grab.py <nasa_id> <orig|large> <start> <duration> <name> [--copy]` reads an HTTP range of a NASA original; `python3 demo/tools/footage.py search|fetch|used|md` searches NASA, Commons and the Internet Archive and records licence, author and page in `SOURCES.jsonl` / `SOURCES.md` automatically. Keep `raw/` under about 1.5 GB.

**Facts**: a `FACTS.md` (claim, URL, quoted wording, or the measurement) covering every number, time, name and call on screen and in the narration; official sources only; planned times and actual (heard) times are kept apart. Check the script against it before the last render.

**Engine** (copy into the project): `demo/index.html` (Canvas 2D: `LAY` layout keyframes with `grid` / `merge` / `cut` / `swap`, `camRegion()` usable regions, `crop()` cover framing, `drawClock()`, `drawTx()`, `drawCheck()`, `drawDoc()`, `drawProfile()`, `drawThrust()`, `window.EV` for the mix, `window.TEXTS` for `readcheck`, `window.SUBFIT` for the one-line subtitle check), `demo/tools/prep.sh` (the sync table → frames), `demo/tools/subs.mjs` (cues → `audio/cues.json`, one-line and duration check), `demo/audio/mix.py` (native sound, ticks, foley, score, ducking, pre-master), `demo/tools/final_asr.py` (Whisper on the finished film), `demo/tools/fetch_fonts.py`.

## 11. Variation space

The agent decides per film: the event, where real time starts and ends, the number of cameras, which documents and data, the control segments, the narrator's lines (or none), the closing layout.

- **Clocks**: T−/T+; a match clock; a wall clock (HH:MM:SS) for a news day; a countdown to a deadline that then counts up as "overtime".
- **Three structures**: rising cells to a merge (this demo); one cell that splits outward after zero (results arriving from many places); two parallel countdowns side by side that meet at zero (two teams, two cities).
- **Three openings**: a single wide shot and the first call; the clock alone on black, then the first camera opens; a document (the schedule) with the first item ticking.
- **Three endings**: the inverted clock over one full-screen shot; the grid refilling with consequences, then one title; the second countdown reaching its own zero.

---

How our demo was made (story, layouts, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

prompts.text:
# Constructivist Montage — Style Prompt

> Real archive footage, photographs and documents, printed as one ink-and-paper poster with a single red, and cut on a machine beat. Diagonal bands carry the type; windows cut along the axis hold the film; people are scissored out of photographs and stacked into structures; numbers count, documents are marked in red, and two images collide to make a third idea.
> References (grammar only): Soviet montage cinema of the 1920s (city symphonies with split screens, counting and machine rhythm; "intellectual" montage where A + B yields a concept), constructivist posters and photomontage (red / black / paper, steep diagonals, photo cut-outs with geometric blocks, type as structure). Never copy their shots, layouts, slogans or lettering, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

1. **Evidence, recut.** Every picture is real material (archive film, photographs, documents) about the actual subject. The film's argument comes from how they are cut and set, not from illustration.
2. **One printed sheet.** All material is converted to the same two-tone print (warm ink → paper); red is the only colour and is laid on top as a printed element.
3. **The beat is the editor.** Cuts, slams, wipes and counts sit on a 120 BPM grid (or the score's tempo); sections accelerate by halving shot length.
4. **Type is structure.** Words and numbers are beams: on a −18° band, as solid blocks, stacked vertically. Never floating captions.
5. **The collective over the individual.** Crowds, hands, machines and many small figures; a single face is never the protagonist.

Not **Data Storytelling** or a keynote: no centred headline with bullets, no slide transitions, no header bars; data appears as marked documents, counters and measured bars inside the composition. Not **Swiss Motion Graphics**: asymmetric, diagonal, no grid of white space, no thin rules as decoration. Not **Art Deco** or **60s Spy Titles**: no gold, no fine lines, no jazz. Not a museum slideshow: archive material is never shown "as is" in a neutral frame; it is cut, windowed, stacked and counted.

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Four kinds of element only**: **bands** (red or ink, along the axis), **windows** (rectangles or parallelograms holding film or photographs), **cut-outs** (people scissored from photographs with a paper-white border), **type blocks**. Plus one paper-fibre texture over everything.
- **The print grade** (one function for film, photos and documents): luminance → percentile stretch (film: one pair of percentiles per clip, so it never pumps; 0.7 / 99.5; photos 0.8 / 99.4) → S-curve `x + s·(x−0.5)·(1−|2x−1|)·2`, s = 0.32 (documents 0.18, they keep their paper) → map to ink→paper: `rgb = INK + (PAPER − INK)·g`. Archive film keeps a ±2.5 % per-frame flicker inside its window (`hash(frame)`), photographs and documents do not.
- **Cut-outs**: a person-segmentation model (u2net_human_seg via onnxruntime) → threshold 0.5 → median filter → largest component → 7 px paper border dilated outside the mask. The border is the medium's own look and hides the model's edge errors. Group photos rarely segment cleanly: use them whole in windows.
- **Documents**: scans at full resolution, never retyped. They are marked: a red highlighter bar in `multiply` over the exact sentence, a hand-drawn red ellipse round a heading, a red circle on a map. Drawings on a document (a chart, a map) may be lifted off the page and reused, keyed from their paper (`alpha = (205 − luminance) / 90`).
- **Resolution ceiling**: archive film ≤ 2.5× its source pixels on screen, modern footage ≤ 1.5×, photos ≥ 1 source px per screen px where possible. Prepare clips with `hqdn3d → lanczos → light unsharp` before grading; add grain only in the mux. A 720-line film transfer can fill a 1,700 px window, not a full 1080p frame: frame it (a window, a split strip, an iris) instead of stretching it.
- **Paper fibre**: a fixed seeded noise canvas multiplied over the frame at α 0.5; film grain 4 added by `mux.sh`.

## 3. Colour logic

| Role | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Red | `#D52B1E` | bands, wedges, blocks, the key number, marker bars, circles and leaders, the one winner in a comparison |
| Ink | `#141210` | type, beams under each floor, window borders, dark grounds |
| Paper | `#EDE4D0` | ground, reversed type, cut-out borders |

- Everything photographic is ink-on-paper; nothing else has colour. Red is never laid on red: a red block on a red ground becomes ink.
- Alternate grounds to make cuts land: paper scene → ink scene → paper. In an acceleration the background itself alternates red / ink per cut.

## 4. Type & subtitles

| Use | Face | Size (1080p) |
|---|---|---|
| Chinese display, slogans | Noto Sans SC 900 (subset) | 110–210 px; stacked vertically 170 px per character |
| Numbers, English display | Oswald 600–700 | numbers 230–440 px; English lines 30–62 px, letter-spacing 2–10 px, capitals |
| Source and footage tags | Space Mono Bold (CJK falls back to Noto) | 17–18 px on an ink or red tab, padding 6 |
| Subtitles | Noto Sans SC 700 40 px over Oswald 500 28 px | bottom left, ink bar at 90 %, a 10 px red tick |

- **Bilingual pairs**: Chinese block, then one English line in Oswald directly under it (or on the neighbouring band). Each language one line, measured.
- **Placement**: along the −18° axis on a band, or as an ink / red block; never centred on the frame, never a header. Numbers can be bigger than the words that explain them.
- **Tags**: every archive window carries its footage tag (`FILM · <TITLE> · <PLACE> <YEAR>`, `PHOTO · <AUTHOR> <YEAR>`), every fact a source tag (`来源 · <PUBLISHER> <YEAR>`). If the footage is not of the subject itself, the tag says what it really is.
- **Subtitles** stay bottom-left in a 960–1056 px strip; key type keeps above y 930 while narration runs. Subtitles hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s). On-screen text follows `readcheck.mjs` (CJK ÷ 4.5 + other ÷ 15 + 1.5 s, fully in frame); a comparison holds every item ≥ 2.5 s before its verdict.

## 5. Edit grammar

- **Grid**: one tempo for picture and score (120 BPM: beat 0.5 s, bar 2 s). Every cut, slam, wipe and count lands on a beat, half-beat or sixteenth. The page exports these times as `window.EV`; the mix reads the same list.
- **Shot length**: 0.5–2 s for footage; one idea per shot. A section may accelerate by halving: 0.5 → 0.25 → 0.125 s (never shorter than 3 frames). Holds are reserved for reading: a text block, a freeze, a comparison.
- **Cut rule**: adjacent shots conflict in at least one of direction (left slam / right slam), value (paper / ink ground), or geometry (diagonal band / upright window). Never two paper documents in a row.
- **Nothing static for more than a second**: inside a hold something moves (film in its window, a counter, a slow push, a frame-within-the-frame). Planned exceptions only: the comparison hold, one silence beat, the end card.
- **Transitions inside the medium** (pick per cut, don't fade):
  - *red wipe*: a 260 px red band at 72° (perpendicular to the axis) sweeps the frame in 0.25 s, the next scene revealed behind it; it lands on the downbeat;
  - *iris*: a red marker circle drawn on a map or photo becomes an aperture and opens onto footage;
  - *slam*: the next element arrives from outside along the axis in 0.08–0.2 s, ease-out, hard stop, frame shake (amplitude 3–18 px, `exp(−14·Δt)`);
  - *flash cut*: one frame of 50–80 % paper over a window at a cut or freeze;
  - *hard cut on the beat* between grounds of opposite value;
  - *jump-in*: inside a freeze, a cut to a 1.2× crop of the same frame, the annotation scaling with it.
- **Two silences**: one where the orchestra stops and only an original recording remains, and one true half-bar of nothing (ink frame, one red dot) before the heaviest hit.

## 6. Formats (each is a function in `demo/index.html`)

| Format | How it looks | How it is built |
|---|---|---|
| **Title package** | a red band slams along the axis; a window cut to the band's edge runs footage; digits stamp one per eighth, the CJK unit in red | `S1`: window clipped to the band's top edge (`onBar`), digits measured and slammed individually, `reg()` registers the group for readcheck |
| **Lower third** | a red bar from the left edge with Chinese, an ink tab with the English | 92 px bar at y ≈ 760–850, slams in 0.14 s, slides off with the next transition |
| **Map + iris** | a document map pushes in, a red circle is drawn round the place, the circle opens onto the site | `mapXf()` (scale / focus / angle over time), `mapToScreen()` keeps the circle on the map point; aperture = `arc` clip whose radius grows to the frame |
| **Vertical title** | CJK characters stacked top to bottom beside a tall window, English rotated 90° | per-character slams 1/16 apart |
| **Date on a girder** | the date in paper on a red band crossing the footage | text placed on the band's centre line (point + normal offset), rotated by the axis |
| **Grid** | 3 × 3 windows light one per sixteenth in a spiral, the centre counts 1…9 and lights last in red | cells `back()`-scale in, each a different clip at 1.4–1.8× speed, ping-pong |
| **Split strips** | the frame rotated to the axis, three strips of two panels each; one panel changes per beat; strips drift in opposite directions | panels ≤ 1,160 px wide so the film stays ≤ 2.5×; red seam on the middle strip |
| **Freeze + annotation** | flash, freeze, push; a red ellipse drawn on the object, a leader to a red block with the number; a jump-in; the film keeps running in a small red-framed inset | the circle is computed from the zoom focus so it follows the jump; inset = same clip, live |
| **Document close-up** | a tilted page slams in, a red marker bar crosses the exact sentence, a red block repeats the number huge | marker in `multiply` over the scan's own line coordinates; a tall slot beside it runs footage fast to show speed |
| **Process staircase** | three windows rising along a diagonal, red triangles between them, a counter climbing to the claim | each window 0.75 s apart; the counter is graphic, only its end value is a fact |
| **The question** | a document heading on an ink ground, circled in red; a huge red "?" | heading cropped tight so only the words that matter show |
| **Acceleration + count** | full-frame windows tilted ±4–6°, ground alternating red / ink, a four-digit counter jumping per cut | cut list with shrinking durations; the original sound plays alone |
| **Multiple exposure** | top-down footage, a second clip in `screen` at 45 %, cut-outs in `multiply`, the answer in a block | exposure window ≤ 1,700 px on a red ground |
| **Chart from the document** | the page turns 90°, its drawings lift off and stand on one ground line to scale, red dimension lines, numbers, names; held; then the verdict block | outlines keyed from the scan, scaled so tip-to-ground = value × px per unit; the winner tinted red (`source-in`) |
| **Photomontage tower** (signature) | floors of footage strips slam in from alternate sides every sixteenth, an ink beam under each, a cut-out worker lands on every other; the camera climbs; a crown and a figure on top | `FLOORS` list, camera `y` follows the eased count of built floors; the floor counter runs to the dated anchor, **rests there while its caption is up**, then runs on to the end value |
| **Silence beat** | ink frame, one red rivet | half a bar; the score and foley are gated to zero |
| **Result composition** | huge numbers left, a tall slanted window with the finished subject (camera tilts up it), a tilted photo, a red wedge | numbers slam, the last line restamps the key number on red |

## 7. Sound palette

- **Score**: an original machine ostinato (eighths, minor, e.g. D–D–F–D–A–D–E–F) in spiccato cellos + staccato bassoon, staccato tuba / trombone on the beat, snare sixteenth taps, xylophone for counts (one rising note per lit cell or built floor), horn / trumpet stabs and a short brass motif, timpani rolls into section changes, gran cassa + gong on the heaviest hit. Sampled CC0 libraries (VSCO 2 CE, VCSL). No piano-and-strings bed.
- **Original sound alternates with music**: in one section the orchestra stops and a real recording (a rivet gun, a machine, a crowd) carries the cut alone, each burst trimmed to its shot. Bring it in a beat early (J-cut).
- **Foley for every printed action**: slam = low thump + steel clank; stamp = thump + clack; wipe and iris = whoosh; marker = filtered noise scrub; paper = band-passed rustle; floors and cells = pitched clanks.
- **Layers**: ambience (a real site / street recording, about 20 dB under the voice, out for the silence), foley ducked 35 % under speech, music ducked 70 % under speech (≈ 10 dB under the voice), narration compressed and levelled by RMS. Master to −14 LUFS with the peaks limited to −1.8 dBFS before `mux.sh`, and a 25 ms fade at sample 0 (an AAC encode overshoots on a hit at the first sample).
- **Narration** (when the film has one): short declarative lines, newsreel cadence, never more than one sentence over a format; numbers spelled out for TTS, digits in subtitles.

## 8. Native moves

1. **The document is marked, not quoted**: the actual sentence on the scan gets a red bar; the number then becomes a red block.
2. **The document becomes the chart**: drawings printed on a page are lifted off, turned and stood on a ground line to scale.
3. **A + B → idea**: two kinds of image alternate faster and faster (the machine / the hands; a heading / the people it leaves out) until a card or a number states what the collision meant.
4. **Count the many**: a counter driven by the cuts, a grid that fills cell by cell, a tower floor by floor.
5. **People build the structure**: cut-out figures stacked into the thing they made (photomontage).
6. **Silence, then the heaviest hit** into the result.

## 9. Footage

1. **Ask first.** Before searching, ask the user for their own material: film, video, photographs, scans of documents (reports, brochures, letters, minutes), data. What they give leads; archives fill gaps.
2. **Where to look, and how to judge the licence** (`demo/tools/footage.py` searches, downloads and records licence, author and source page into `SOURCES.jsonl`; `footage.py md` writes `SOURCES.md`):
   - **Internet Archive**: read each item's `licenseurl` and description. Public Domain Mark / CC0 / CC BY are usable; *no licence field* is not. For a pre-1978 US film, check the title and end cards for a copyright notice: published 1930 or earlier = public domain in the US by date; published without notice before 1978 = public domain; with a notice, check renewal. Corroborate date and producer elsewhere (a library catalogue, an archive exhibit). Avoid YouTube mirrors, re-uploads with no provenance, colourised or "restored" versions.
   - **Wikimedia Commons**: read the file page's licence and its source institution. Public domain, CC0, CC BY (credit in full) are usable; CC BY-SA is not used in library demos.
   - **US National Archives (NARA)**, **Library of Congress**, **NASA**, other US federal agencies: federal works are public domain; check each item's rights statement. "No known restrictions" (LOC, Flickr Commons) is **not** clear enough: name it to the user or find the same image elsewhere with a clear statement.
   - **Museums with open access** (Met, Rijksmuseum, Smithsonian): CC0 where the object page says so; check that the item is still marked open access.
   - **University and city libraries** (e.g. Columbia's digitised ephemera on the Internet Archive): use their rights statement; "copyright status undetermined" is not usable.
3. **Tell the user before downloading**: what (title, years), from where (URL), under which licence and why. Keep `raw/` under about 1.5 GB; download serially (Commons rate-limits).
4. Record every asset with the seconds used (`footage.py used <name> "<source s> → film s"`), list it in `demo/CREDITS`, and keep the trail for anything judged "no notice".
5. Footage that is not of the subject itself (another city, another year) may stand in only with a tag that says exactly what it is.

## 10. Facts

Every number, date and claim on screen or in the voice comes from an official or primary source (a contemporary report, an official brochure, a government record), kept in `demo/FACTS.md` with the URL and the quoted wording. Counters are graphics: only their end values and dated anchors are facts. Where two primary sources disagree (a film's intertitle vs. the official brochure), use one and record the conflict.

## 11. Engine

- `demo/index.html`: one Canvas 2D page, stateless `render(t)`; scene functions draw a full frame; wipes draw the old scene, clip, draw the new one, then the band. `txt()` draws and registers rotated text boxes for `readcheck.mjs`; `reg()` registers a group drawn in pieces; `slam()`, `flash()`, `flicker()`, `shake()`, `slant()` (parallelogram windows), `cover()` (focus-point cover fit), `clipImg()` (forward / reverse / ping-pong / speed).
- `demo/tools/prep.py`: the print grade, clip extraction to 24 fps JPEG sequences (one percentile set per clip), stills, document pages and outline keying, cut-outs. `demo/tools/fonts.py`: fetch the OFL fonts and subset Noto Sans SC to the characters used. `demo/tools/cues.mjs`: subtitle cues from the page's own table, measured one line per language. `demo/audio/mix.py`: score, foley, narration, ambience, master.
- Checks: `readcheck.mjs`, `asr_check.py` per line, `tools/final_asr.py` on the final mix, `tools/rhythm_report.py` (flat windows, cut points, hit-to-onset alignment), `mux.sh` loudness.

## 12. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Upscaled archive film** turns to mush on a 1080p full frame: window it; split strips into panels; keep zooms inside the 2.5× ceiling.
- **Per-frame grading pumps**: one percentile pair per clip.
- **Type on a band running off frame**: place it from the band's centre line (point + normal), not by eye.
- **Red on red**: a red answer block on a red exposure ground disappears; switch it to ink.
- **A face as hero**: ordinary identifiable workers appear in groups, at work, in quick cuts; no slow motion or close-up protagonist.
- **Counters read as facts**: label only the end value and dated anchors; a caption beside a counter must match the number shown at every frame (stop the count on the caption's value while it is up).
- **A number without a unit**: every counter carries its unit in the same layout as elsewhere (小时 / 层 / 人 MEN).
- **Ink type over a window**: a line that runs past a photo's edge disappears into dark film; give it a paper tab or keep it clear of the window.
- **The verdict covering what was compared**: place it where no item is, after the hold.
- **Too many documents**: one marked sentence per document shot; a page with three highlights is a slide.
- **Short labels in an acceleration** fail reading time by design: keep text out of the 1/8-beat cuts; put the result in a held block after.
- **A hit at sample 0** overshoots in the AAC encode: fade the first 25 ms.

## 13. Variation space

The agent decides per film: structure, which archive and documents, which formats (not all of them in one film), the axis angle (−15° to −30°), the red's exact hue, tempo (100–140 BPM), whether there is narration (intertitles only is valid), the signature build (a tower, a bridge span, a crowd forming a word, a map filling in).

- **Three structures:** a calendar machine (one counter runs the whole film and stops at milestones); a document that asks and footage that answers (the turn at the middle); one object's journey through a process, then the scale of the whole.
- Subjects that fit: construction and engineering histories, industrial anniversaries, mass events, labour and collective effort, infrastructure openings, any "many people, one machine rhythm" story with archive film and documents behind it.

Our demo: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md).

prompts.text:
# Broadcast News Package — Style Prompt

> A television newsroom's on-air package, built entirely in code: a sting that becomes the channel bug, a rundown of today's stories that opens and closes the bulletin, a lower-third strap that never leaves the bottom of the frame, and full-frame graphics (split-flap price boards, a line breaking a threshold, explainer maps, documents flying out of a city, quote cards, spec cards with proportion bars, stamps) that carry the facts. The style is the **package system plus its cutting rules**, not a drawing style. 16:9, a clean frame: no burned-in subtitles, no news crawl.
> References (grammar only): evening network news headline menus, financial-channel market graphics, European news channels' explainer maps, tech-desk spec cards. Never copy a broadcaster's logo, set, fonts, colours, music or idents, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

1. **One package system, used consistently.** Every graphic is built from the same few parts: a brand plate (parallelogram), a tab in the accent colour, a paper strap, ink cards with an accent top edge, mono datelines, stamps. Viewers read the system before they read the words.
2. **The bulletin's order.** Sting → rundown ("today we have four stories") → item → item → … → back to the rundown, ticked off → sign-off. Each item opens with its category on the strap's tab and its date on the first graphic.
3. **One fact per screen.** A full-frame graphic states one thing: the price, the break, the two stocks, the place, the two letters, the quote, the verdict.
4. **The strap holds the headline.** One lower-third strap is on screen from the first story to the recap and changes its words with a vertical flip; the picture above it is free for the graphic.
5. **Clean panel.** No crawl, no burned-in subtitles; subtitles ship as a separate `.srt`. The frame is the graphic, the strap, the bug and a source line.

Not **Caption News** (that is captions-first social video: huge slammed captions are the lead, no rundown, no strap; here type is small and orderly and the graphics lead). Not **Data Storytelling** (one chart per beat, never a dashboard; the chart is an insert in a bulletin). Not a keynote: no centred title-and-bullets, no page turns. Not a studio show: no virtual set, no anchor, no fly-throughs — the package is flat graphics over ink.

## 2. Frame and layout (1920×1080)

| Zone | Position | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Content | x 96–1824, y 56–840 | the full-frame graphic; when a strap is up, nothing important below y 840 |
| Lower-third strap | tab x 96 y 856, 48 high; strap x 96 y 904, 1250×104, + 120 px ink end block | category tab (accent, ink text, Chinese + English), headline in Chinese 50 px + one English line 27 px |
| Source line | right-aligned at x 1836, y 950 / 978 | `SOURCE: …` mono 13 px + Chinese 16 px, 75 % opacity; English ≤ 36 characters or it slides under the strap's end block |
| Channel bug | top right, plate centre (1739, 86), 0.327 of the sting plate | the plate plus `AI NEWS` |
| Corner tag | top left x 96 y 56, 330×64 | `ILLUSTRATION / 示意 · AI 生成画面` on generated plates, `SCHEMATIC / 示意图` on schematic charts; flips in and out 0.2 s |

Content layers sit lower than a subtitled layout would put them (a 60–110 px downward shift) so the bottom strap does not leave an empty band above it. When you remove subtitles and the crawl, re-lay the page; never leave the space they used.

## 3. Package parts (specs)

| Part | Spec | Rules |
|---|---|---|
| Sting | 0–1.5 s | two accent slashes (0.04, 0.10 s) → the plate slams in with an overshoot, an impact ring and shake (0.16–0.42) → letters drop in one by one → wordmark and dateline open from the centre → a glint → the plate flies to the top right and **becomes the bug** while a vertical band wipes into the first shot. A hit within 0.4 s |
| Brand plate | parallelogram 520×180, accent gradient, ink and gold bars at the left, name in condensed 800 | the same object is the sting, the bug, the desk front and the end card |
| Rundown | left: date block (big numerals, month, week); right: three rows, 1024×140, number block in accent | rows flip in vertically on the beat (back ease) with a glint; at the close the same object returns and each row is ticked |
| Lower-third strap | see §2 | enters with the first story, flips (new words up from below, old up and out, 0.32 s; the tab flashes white when the category changes), leaves with a slide when the recap starts. A **profile** version (tab `人物 PROFILE`) names a speaker |
| Split-flap board | tiles 220×130, top and bottom halves clipped separately | old value and new value on the same board, so the change reads in one look; ×2 / +x % called out to the right |
| Threshold chart | line from the peak, the threshold as a dashed gold line | the line head advances one trading day per step; the last step crosses the threshold in accent with a shake and a ring; the readout panel slides in after; axes show only what the data supports |
| Bars | grow from a zero line downward for losses, values roll | a reference line at the shared threshold plus a badge |
| Explainer map | the same projection, one long take | members light in order of distance from the city; the city label, the institution label with leader, a stamp; the camera pushes, then pans to make room |
| Documents | 380×490 paper, ink header | fly out of the city dot on an arc (0.5 s, scale 0.08 → 1, rotation settles); check boxes tick on the voice's key words |
| Quote card | ink background with the package's light streaks, a large accent quotation mark lands first, lines push up one by one (0.18 s apart), then the Chinese gist, a gold rule, name, occasion and date | the official wording, in the language it was said; never paraphrase inside quotation marks; an underline sweeps the key word as the voice says it |
| Spec card | eyebrow (source · date), the product name pushed up from a mask, a category stamp, proportion bars on one scale (the whole vs the part, values rolling), a percentage badge, a context chip; a second group on the right for the hardware or the place, filling cell by cell, joined by a bracket to its total | one scale for every bar, so the proportion is true; every number from the source page |
| Stamps | accent fill or ink with a double accent frame, −6° to −10° | land from 1.9× in 0.16 s with an expanding ellipse; one per story at most |
| Transitions | vertical band wipe (accent 84 px + ink 5 px + gold 14 px edge, 0.3 s) between stories and programme parts; hard cut + timpani inside a story; slanted wipe into the end card | nothing else: no dissolves, no 3D flips, no page turns, no fly-throughs. **The package layer travels with its picture**: under a wipe each side draws its own strap words, tab, source line and corner tag (old state on the old side, new state on the new side), so the band brushes the headline over; on a hard cut they change on the same frame. Strap words never flip or overlap. The incoming picture's entry animation starts under the band, so its first revealed frame already has content |

## 4. Colour

| Role | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| ink | `#121417` | backgrounds, panels, strap end block |
| ink2 / ink3 | `#1B1E23` / `#22262C` | cards, land on maps |
| accent (lemon) | `#F2CF1D` (light `#F8DE4A`, dark `#D8B30C`) | plate, tabs, band wipe, bars, stamps, the line that breaks |
| gold | `#D4B064` | thresholds, datelines, source lines, light fins, badges |
| paper | `#F4F1E8` | strap, documents, the chart line |
| breaking | `#FE6B3D` | only for BREAKING and LIVE. A weekly round-up has neither, so it never appears |

Structure to keep when you change the brand: one accent + one gold-like secondary + paper + ink, and a reserved alarm colour. Ink text on the accent; on paper, English secondary lines in a dark olive (`#6E5A1E`) because gold is too weak there.

## 5. Type

- Chinese: Noto Sans SC 900 (headlines, strap) / 700 (labels).
- Latin: Barlow Condensed 800 (numbers, names, the plate), 600 (secondary lines, quotes), 600 italic (the end-card English title).
- Mono: IBM Plex Mono 500 for datelines, sources, axis labels, all caps with 1–4 px tracking.
- All OFL, subset from Google Fonts by `demo/tools/fonts.sh` (the character list is read from `main.js`; delete `fonts/*.woff2` after a text change). No handwriting faces in this style.
- Every label is bilingual on one line each (Chinese first, English smaller); never wrap.

## 6. Picture layer and grade

- When there is no footage, the picture layer is data graphics drawn in code plus, at most, a few **illustrative plates** (generated or stock), each tagged `ILLUSTRATION` for as long as it is on screen. They set a mood (a server room behind a model launch, a wafer behind chip stocks); they never stand in for the event, the place or the people.
- One grade for every plate: greyscale → auto black/white points (0.5 / 99.6 percentile) → γ 1.05 → 35 % S-curve → black 8, white 232 → duotone `#0E1013` → `#ECE7D8` (`tools/prep.py: grade()`), plus a left-dark ink gradient for type, a 50–55 % vignette and 7 % overlay grain cycling through six tiles. Graphics and the package are never grained.
- Real footage, if you have it, takes the same grade path; modern footage ≤ 1.5× scale, archive ≤ 2.5× after deblocking; crop out station logos.

## 7. Editing grammar

- **120 BPM grid**, beat 0 at the end of the sting (1.5 s). Every cut and wipe on a beat or half-beat.
- **Shot lengths**: sting 1.5 s; rundown 4–5 s; story shots 3–7 s; a map long take (6–12 s) as the bulletin's breath; a comparison stays until every item has been fully on screen ≥ 2.5 s.
- **A package action every 0.5–1 s** inside a shot (flip, count, stamp, tick, strap change, map light, line step). No frame flat for more than 1 s; a strong action within 0.5 s of every cut.
- **Date every story**: a weekly bulletin's items happen on different days; the date sits in the rundown row, the eyebrow line, the readout or the document.
- **The order inside an item**: what (the name or the number) → how big (the line, the bars, the price board) → who it hits or who said it (bars, documents, a quote) → the verdict stamp.

## 8. Sound palette

| Layer | What | Level |
|---|---|---|
| Anchor voice | one narrator, one sentence per graphic, starting 0.1 s after the cut; HP 90 Hz, 3:1 compression. Default: the library's Kokoro (`core/tts/tts.py`, free, Apache 2.0) in English or Chinese. The user's own recording, or another TTS they have a key for (for example Doubao, as in the demo), replaces it — never required | music ducked ≈ −7 dB and its 1.2–5 kHz band thinned under speech |
| News theme | 120 BPM, minor key: spiccato violins in root–fifth–octave eighths, pizzicato bass on the beat, horn pads, a low-passed 16th-note saw pulse, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4 | full under the rundown and the first story |
| Section moods | markets: violins down an octave, tremolo, four-on-the-floor kick (heartbeat); policy: pizzicato and horns only | |
| Signature hits | sting tutti; glockenspiel notes as the rundown rows land; timpani on hard cuts and story changes; one beat of silence before the biggest break, then the heaviest hit of the film; a held drone after the verdict stamp; a major-key lift for the last story; tutti on the end card | |
| Foley | whoosh on wipes, flap clicks on split-flaps, stamp thump + clack, trading-room ticks under market charts, map clicks per lit country, a sonar ping on a city, paper and typewriter ticks on documents, click + glockenspiel on ticks | |
| Room | server-room hum under a tech plate, soft air under maps | very low |

Master −14 LUFS, true peak −1.2 dB (`core/render/mux.sh`). Samples: VSCO 2 CE and VCSL (CC0); foley synthesised (`core/audio/sfx.py`).

## 9. Native moves

1. **Sting becomes the bug** — the brand plate slams in, then flies to the corner and stays there for the whole bulletin; opening and programme are one object.
2. **Strap tab = category** — the strap's tab changes category (模型 MODELS, 市场 MARKETS, 监管 POLICY …) with a white flash when a new story starts; no separate item cards between stories.
3. **Rundown, then ticked off** — the same list opens and closes the bulletin; at the end each row gets its tick.
4. **Spec card** — a launch reduced to its proportions: the whole and the part on one scale, then what it runs on, joined by a bracket to the total.
5. **Strap that never leaves** — one strap group from the first story to the recap; words flip, the strap itself never exits mid-programme.
6. **Split-flap before/after** — old and new value on one board, each tile flipping from the old to the new.
7. **Breaking the threshold** — a line advances one period per step towards a dashed threshold; the music stops for one beat before the last step and the crossing gets the heaviest hit.
8. **Date in the eyebrow** — every graphic's eyebrow line carries source and date in mono caps, so a weekly round-up never blurs which day each item happened.
9. **City sends the letters** — on a map long take, documents fly out of the sending city to their addressees; one world→screen function keeps labels and documents attached through push and pan.
10. **Quote card + verdict stamp** — the official's own words in type, with name, occasion and date; an underline on the key word as the voice says it; one stamp.

Where each move lives in the demo's code: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md) (build notes).

## 10. Material

1. **Facts first.** Every on-screen number and every sentence of the voice comes from an official source (the company's own page, the exchange's data, the institution's press release or speech), recorded in `demo/FACTS.md` with claim, URL, quoted wording and any arithmetic. When a fact exists only in a news report, attribute it on screen and in the voice ("据…报道 / … reports") and keep to the plain claim; never put a single report's allegations about a real company or person on screen.
2. **Data.** Draw charts from real series only; when you have just a few reported numbers, draw a *schematic* line, tag it `SCHEMATIC`, and label only what you know. Exchange closes: the exchange itself, the central bank's statistics portal, or a market-data file whose source you log.
3. **Pictures: ask in this order.**
   a. **The user's own images** — photos, b-roll stills, their logo and colours (the package is rebuilt around their brand). Use these first.
   b. **Generated illustrative plates**, if the user wants them. Before generating, tell the user how many images and what each shows (one line per plate). With the Codex CLI installed and able to generate images, `demo/tools/gen_image.py` (driven by `demo/tools/gen_plates.sh`) makes them and saves JPEGs to `demo/assets/plates/`. With any other image tool (an API or a web app), give the user the prompts and the target file names; they generate the images and drop them into `demo/assets/plates/`. Prompts ask for no text, letters, logos, flags or people.
   c. **No generated images**: public-domain, CC0 or CC BY photographs (licences below), or abstract backgrounds drawn in code (gradients, grids, light fins — the package already carries the frame).
   Whatever the source: every word on screen is typeset in code, never baked into an image; a generated plate is only ever an illustration behind a graphic, tagged `ILLUSTRATION / 示意` for as long as it is visible, and never stands in for the event, a place in the news, or a person. No generated anchor.
4. **Photo and footage licences** (judge each file on its own page, not the search result):
   - **Wikimedia Commons**: CC0, public domain or CC BY (credit author, title, licence on the end card and in `CREDITS`). Not used: CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions", unclear licences, YouTube re-uploads, colourised or "restored" versions.
   - **U.S. federal agencies** (NASA, NOAA, NARA, USGS…): public domain; check the page does not credit a contractor or third party.
   - **Internet Archive**: only items whose page states public domain, CC0 or CC BY; U.S. works published before 1931 are public domain.
   - **Library of Congress / national archives**: read each rights statement; "no known restrictions" is not enough.
   - **Institutions' audiovisual services** (for example the European Commission's): read their reuse terms per item; many require attribution and forbid implying endorsement.
   - **Maps**: Natural Earth (public domain), via `world-atlas` TopoJSON.
5. **Before downloading, tell the user** what you will fetch, from where and under which licence. The finder copied into this style, `demo/tools/footage.py` (`search commons|archive|nasa`, `fetch`, `used`, `md`), logs licence, author, page and the seconds used into `SOURCES.jsonl` and writes `SOURCES.md`. Keep `raw/` under ~1.5 GB.
6. **Logos**: never use a company's logo for a company in the news; set its name in type.
7. **People**: public figures in the news can be named on a profile strap; no close-up or slow motion of private individuals.
8. **Voice and music**: ask whether the user has a recorded anchor, a preferred voice or a theme of their own before synthesising one.

## 11. Pitfalls

- **Package left behind.** If the strap, source line or tags are drawn once on top of everything, a wipe changes the picture under yesterday's headline and the strap catches up 0.3–0.5 s later. Draw them per picture, inside the wipe's clip.
- **Leftover layout.** Removing subtitles or a crawl without moving the content down leaves a dead band above the strap.
- **Masked type peeking in.** A push-in title clipped by a mask shows its top edge before it moves if the travel distance doesn't clear the mask; start it fully below and don't draw at progress 0.
- **Words stronger than the source.** "Request for information" is not "investigation" or "penalty"; write "no fine, no case opened" or "for the first time" only if a source says so — and check the institution's own pages, which can contradict a report ("first requests" may have gone out months earlier).
- **Thresholds depend on the reference.** "Bear market" = −20 % from *which* high? Name the reference on the axis; from a different peak the claim can be false.
- **Attribute what only a report says.** When the official source does not name the companies, the graphic carries "据… 报道 / reported by …" and so does the voice.
- **A schematic posing as data.** Rolling counters on a close price flash values that never existed; set the close with a mask push instead. Don't label axes the data doesn't support.
- **Source lines under the strap.** Right-aligned mono 13 px: ≤ 36 characters.
- **Stamps over key words.** A stamp hit can mask the voice ("fines"); take the brass off the stamp and low-pass its clack.
- **Gold on paper** has too little contrast: use ink or dark olive.
- **Generated plates** carry stray corner marks: crop them in `prep.py`.
- **Short preview text.** Rundown rows are previews of the stories; `readcheck` flags them as short in the opening — they return in the recap and as straps, so accept the flag or leave them out of `TEXTS`.
- **Names in synthetic speech.** Spell brand names, model numbers and abbreviations the way they should sound in the TTS text (a respelling, a number written as a word, an abbreviation without dots) while the strap and subtitles keep the real spelling; when speech-to-text mishears an unusual name, put the expected transcript in the line's `asr` field instead of rewriting the line.

## 12. Variation space

Decide per film: the channel's name, plate and accent colour; how many items (one lead with a long package, three or four equal items, a five-item round-up); which full-frame graphics each item needs; where the long take goes; the anchor's voice.

- **Three structures:** rundown → items → rundown ticked (round-up); one lead package with a correspondent two-box and a short "also today" grid; a countdown of items (election-night, sports results).
- **Three openings:** sting → rundown; cold open on the biggest graphic, then the sting; sting straight into the first story with the rundown as a recap only.
- **Three endings:** rundown ticked → end card; a "coming up next week" teaser card; the last stamp freezing into the end card.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

prompts.text:
# 1920s Newsreel — Style Prompt

> A sound newsreel of the late 1920s, cut from real archive material: a searchlight-and-globe ident with a brass fanfare, a newspaper that spins into the lens, a fast and cheerful announcer on an optical soundtrack, place-and-date cards, maps, magazine pages and documents, wipes, flips and irises, and a hot band that can stop dead for the punchline.
> References (grammar only): **Fox Movietone News** and **Universal Newspaper Newsreel** (1927–1930s) — the ident ritual, the announcer's patter, one story per location, the stinger after the last story; **Pathé News** — the item title card; Hollywood's **spinning newspaper** montage; **1920s hot dance bands** (Charleston rhythm, banjo, tuba). Never copy a real newsreel's name, logo, globe design, typeface or fanfare.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

An edit style: the look is in **how real material is arranged, cut, captioned and carried by sound**, not in a drawing technique.
- **Archive in a projected gate**: 1.37:1 picture, full height, rounded corners, black outside; everything inside it shares one silver grade, gate weave, flicker, scratches and dust.
- **News objects** do the explaining: newspapers, magazine pages, books, telegrams, maps, records. They are filmed (spun, slammed, panned, turned, underlined), never typeset as slides.
- **A voice talks over everything**: short exclamations, half joking, never a lecture.
- **Music is a band, and it edits**: cuts land on the band's beats; the band stops dead to let a line land; a period record can take over the soundtrack.

Not `silent-film` (1920s Silent Film, in this library): that style is a drawn, inked comedy projected between velvet curtains, with intertitles instead of voices, a cinema pianist and no foley. Here nothing is drawn but the packaging; the footage and print are real; somebody always speaks; the soundtrack is brass, banjo and records; titles are news captions (place · date), not dialogue cards; there are no curtains and no theatre.
Not a documentary with a "vintage filter" either: no talking heads, no slow Ken Burns drifts, no modern lower-third bars.

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Gate**: 1480 × 1080 inside 1920 × 1080 (1.37:1), corner radius 26 px, pure black outside. Nothing is ever drawn outside the gate.
- **Two layers**: the picture layer (footage, print, maps, cards) gets the film look; the type layer (place cards, labels, subtitles, the record inset) stays sharp and steady. Grease-pencil marks belong to the picture (they weave with it).
- **Base grade** for every source, before anything else (`tools/prep.py`, `grade()`): greyscale → percentile stretch (0.6 % → black, 99.6 % → white; print: 0.2–0.3 % / 99.0–99.7 % with the black lifted to 26–30, like newsprint) → mild S-curve `x + 0.18·(x−0.5)·(1−|2x−1|)` → output 14–238. **Moving footage uses one level set per clip** (sampled across all its frames), never per frame.
- **Projection look** (`filmLook()`, picture layer only): warm silver (`multiply #efe7d6`, `screen #17140f`), vignette 0.42 H → 0.95 H, flicker ±3.5 % per frame + 3 Hz drift, gate weave ±1.6 px / ±2.2 px (value noise), 0–3 vertical scratches that live for 9 frames, 0–4 one-frame dust specks. Grain is added at mux (`mux.sh … 24 7`), not in the page.
- **Archive film upscaling**: at most ~2.5×. NTSC transfers (720 × 480) are treated as 4:3, cropped to 1.37 and scaled 2.31× to 1480 × 1080: `hqdn3d=4:3:6:5` → `lanczos` → `unsharp=5:5:0.55` → base grade. Frames are exported at 24 fps as JPEG sequences and played by `floor((t − t0) · 24)`, so renders are deterministic.
- **Print**: newspapers, magazines and books at their scan resolution; crop pages to the relevant fold so unrelated (and sometimes ugly) old stories never come into view.
- **Code-drawn packaging only**: the ident (sunburst, two searchlights, wire globe), item title cards, maps, the end card. Never generate "archive" pictures.

## 3. Colour logic

- **Monochrome warm silver** for the picture; values do the work (check every shot as a thumbnail).
- Type is cream on near-black (`#f3eee4` / `#d6cfc0` on `rgba(12,11,10,.8)`), framed by a 2 px cream rule; marks are a slightly warm white grease pencil; underlines on printed pages are dark soft lead.
- Packaging silver: Art Deco gradient lettering `#fff → #d9d4ca | #9e978a → #efebe2` with a hard "metal" break at the middle and a black outline (0.12 em).
- No colour accents, no sepia wash on top of the silver, no colourised archive.

## 4. Type & subtitles

| Use | Face (all OFL) | Spec |
|---|---|---|
| Ident, item cards, end title | Limelight | 104–118 px, silver gradient, black outline |
| Chinese display (ident, cards, end title) | Noto Serif SC 900 | 50–76 px, letter-spacing 10–26 px, `#ece7dc` |
| Place card, labels (English) | Oswald 600 | 26–34 px, letter-spacing 4–6 px, upper case "PLACE · DATE" |
| Place card, labels (Chinese) | Noto Sans SC 500–600 | 24–30 px |
| Subtitles | Noto Sans SC 600 40 px over Oswald 400 29 px | bottom of the gate (baselines H−82 / H−38), black stroke 8 / 6 px |

- **Place card** (the newsreel's segment title, instead of full-screen cards for every story): top left of the gate (gate x + 48, y 56), dark box with an inset 2 px cream frame, English "PLACE · DATE" over one Chinese line; it is pulled out left to right in 0.22 s and fades 0.15 s before it leaves. Hold ≥ CJK ÷ 4.5 + Latin ÷ 15 + 1.5 s from the moment it is complete (`readcheck.mjs`), so keep both lines short.
- **Item title card** (one per film at most, to turn to a new story): black, a double Art Deco frame drawn in 0.35 s with quarter-fan corners, Limelight line + Chinese line, slow push; ≥ 2.5 s.
- **Labels inside split screens**: one per panel, top centre, same box style, enter one beat apart.
- **Subtitle strip**: the subtitles sit on a dark strip across the bottom of the gate (180 px, transparent at the top edge, ≈ 93–96 % `#0a0908` below), on every shot, fading in 0.25 s before the first cue of a run and held through gaps under 1 s, so it never blinks; print and pale footage would otherwise swallow the letters (`subBand()`).
- **Subtitles**: Chinese line over English line, **one line per language, never wrapped** (`tools/subcheck.mjs` measures every cue in the page); a cue lasts max(1.8 s, spoken + 0.6 s) and ends 50 ms before the next. Print in shot is never re-typed as a caption: the announcer and subtitles carry its meaning, an underline points at it.

## 5. Editing grammar

- **The band is the clock**: pick a hot-dance tempo (190–220 BPM); every cut, landing, slam and label entrance sits on a beat, most cuts on bar lines; quick inserts on beat 3 or on the Charleston accent (beat 1 and the "and" of 2). When a period record plays, cut on the record's own beat (measure it), not on the grid.
- **One story = one place + one kind of material + one line of voice.** Stories get shorter towards the end (2–3 bars → 1 bar → beats), then one held button.
- **Shot lengths**: archive shots 1–2.5 s; print and documents 2.5–4 s (they must be read); comparisons ≥ 2.5 s fully in frame before the verdict; never a static frame longer than ~1 s without something moving (push, roll, pencil, flicker of a counter).
- **Transitions are the newsreel's own, each used once, as punctuation**: iris close/open, diagonal hard wipe with a bright 6 px edge, vertical-axis flip, venetian blinds (12 slats turning), clock wipe from 12 o'clock, spinning paper, page turn, panel push-over, freeze. No cross-dissolves between stories, no modern whip pans, no zoom blur.
- **L-cuts**: the announcer may run 0.3–0.5 s over a cut; a new music state may start one beat before its picture (J-cut).

## 6. Camera on stills and archive

| Move | What it does | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Spin-and-slam | the paper arrives as news | a headline; a telegram; a poster |
| Slow push then punch-in on a beat | from the whole page to the one detail | a headline → a photo in it |
| Pan across a wide print | a crowd, a parade, a skyline | panoramas, group photos |
| Tilt to reveal | the landmark behind the subject | a building, a monument |
| Map push | from the country to one city, into the next story | travel, spread, campaigns |
| Grid deal | many related stills land one per beat | step-by-step, collections, "all of them" |
| Flip-book | a series of stills played on the beat becomes motion | dance steps, assembly stages, before/after |
| Freeze + jolt | stop the archive on the telling frame | the punchline, the evidence |
| Split / quad | two or four places at once, side by side | comparisons, "everybody's doing it" |

Archive footage is not reframed with fake camera moves bigger than ~6 % (it already has its own camera); stills always get a move with a purpose.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Announcer** (Kokoro): a bright, energetic male voice; a blend of two voices (e.g. `am_liam:0.6,bm_george:0.4`) gives a mid-Atlantic tinge; speed ≈ 1.15–1.2; 6–12 words per line, exclamations and rhetorical questions. Treatment as a 1930 optical track (`period_voice()` in `audio/mix.py`): high-pass 260 Hz, low-pass 3.7 kHz, +4 dB presence at 1.5–2.3 kHz (horn loudspeaker), tanh drive 2.0, compression 4:1, wow 0.22 % at 0.55 Hz + flutter 0.07 % at 6.3 Hz, two short wall reflections (31 ms, 67 ms). The speech check runs on the clean voice and again on the finished film (`tools/final_asr.py`).
- **Band** (original): tuba on 1 and 3, banjo four to the bar (accent 2 and 4), trombones on the Charleston figure (1 and the "and" of 2), snare backbeat, honky-tonk piano right hand, muted then open trumpet melody with clarinet a sixth below, woodblock pickups; a brass fanfare with timpani for the ident; a dead stop with one stab for the punchline; "da – DA!" to close.
- **Counter-music**: when the story has two sides, give the other side its own band (here an old-time reel: fiddle, plucked dulcimer, upright piano, tuba) and let them trade bars, then half bars, in a split screen, panned left and right.
- **Archive record**: a public-domain 78 can take over the soundtrack as "the real thing": needle drop (click + surface noise), band-pass 110–6500 Hz, crackle and rotation rumble only while the needle is down, varispeed by ≤ 2 % to sit on the film's tempo; end it on its own final chord and lift the needle.
- **Foley** for every move: carbon-arc snap, rising whoosh with flutter for the spinning paper, thump + paper slap, telegraph clicks under a map line, camera shutter per still, paper flicks per flip-book page, slat flutter, page turn, grease-pencil squeak, soft-lead scratch.
- **Bed**: projector (24 Hz claw clatter, motor hum, optical hiss) from first to last frame.
- **Mix**: the band and record ducked ≈ 4–5 dB under the voice (voice ≈ 12 dB over the music), the band band-limited 95–7500 Hz with a low shelf and light saturation; two silences (a dead stop before a turn, only the projector before the button); −14 LUFS.

## 8. Native moves

A menu; use the ones the story needs, each once.

- **The ident ritual.** Searchlights snap on with a flash in the first 0.2 s, the globe grows and turns, the name lands with overshoot, the iris closes on the globe. Code: `sceneLogo()` — `sunburst()`, `beams()`, `globe()`, `decoTitle()`. *Fits:* the opening of any news-shaped film; the reprise is the sign-off.
- **The spinning paper.** Grows by `u^2.3`, rotation decays by `(1−u)^1.25` over 2.5 turns, three ghost copies 18 ms apart as motion blur, a vertical jolt (damped sine, 16 px) and a 3 % bounce on the slam, then push and punch in on the next beat. *Fits:* a headline, a decree, a press release.
- **The map spread.** A projected outline (Natural Earth, Albers), dotted arcs from the source city drawn on the beat with telegraph clicks, star pulses on arrival, place labels in screen space, an odometer of years in a corner; push into the city of the next story. *Fits:* a craze, a product launch, a migration, a campaign.
- **Grid deal → flip-book.** Stills land one per beat (shutter click each), then the camera dives into the first cell and the series plays on the beat as stop motion. *Fits:* a how-to, the stages of a process, a collection.
- **Document underline.** Slam a book or letter, turn the page, push to the paragraph, draw soft-lead underlines word-exact (positions from the scan's OCR boxes, e.g. archive.org hOCR). *Fits:* a quote, a rule, a contract clause.
- **Grease-pencil freeze.** Freeze the telling frame, jolt it, ring the detail with a hand-drawn loop (`pencil()` + `ring()`), add an arrow. *Fits:* the evidence, the punchline, "look here".
- **Split-screen duel → push-over.** Two panels slide in, each labelled, each with its own music in its own channel trading bars; the winner pushes the loser out of frame. *Fits:* old vs new, rival products, two cities.
- **Needle drop.** The band cuts dead, a 78 spins in the corner, the period record plays under the archive and ends on its own chord at the freeze. *Fits:* any era that has public-domain recordings.
- **Band stop + button.** One stab, silence with only the projector, one short line from the announcer. *Fits:* the last word of any story.

## 9. Material: where it comes from

1. **Ask the user first** whether they have their own material: film or video, photographs, newspapers, letters, documents, data, a period recording. Their archive beats anything found online.
2. **If not, search sources whose licence is clear**, with `demo/tools/footage.py` (`search archive|commons|nasa`, `files`, `fetch`, `used`, `md`; it records licence, author and page in `SOURCES.jsonl`):
   - **U.S. National Archives** (films, often via Internet Archive "FedFlix" copies): federal works are public domain; donated collections need their own rights note (e.g. the Ford Motor Company Film Collection: all rights transferred to NARA in 1962, "copyright- and royalty-free" except contractor films). Universal Newsreel (1929–1967) is in NARA too.
   - **Internet Archive**: check every item's licence field and provenance; skip anything that is a YouTube mirror, a colourised or "restored/AI enhanced" version, or has no stated source.
   - **Wikimedia Commons**: read the licence template on the file page; use PD-US-expired, PD-US-no-notice, PD-USGov, CC0, CC BY. A Library of Congress "No known restrictions" (often with "Copyright-tag-still-required") is **not** enough, nor is DPLA "no known restrictions"; CC BY-SA is not used in library demos.
   - **Library of Congress** (loc.gov, tile.loc.gov; Chronicling America newspapers before 1931), **NASA**, other national archives.
   - **Print**: anything published in the US before 1931 (newspapers, magazines, books on archive.org / HathiTrust / Commons) is public domain in the US.
   - **Recordings**: US sound recordings published before 1926 are public domain in the US from 1 January 2026 (Music Modernization Act: 100 years after publication for pre-1947 recordings); UCSB Library / Internet Archive transfers (Edison, Victor) and the LOC National Jukebox give dates and matrix numbers. Check the composition's date too.
   - **Maps**: Natural Earth (public domain) for outlines drawn in code.
3. **Before downloading, tell the user** what you will fetch, from where, under which licence, and how big it is; keep `raw/` under ~1.5 GB.
4. Everything used goes into `demo/CREDITS` and `SOURCES.md` (title, author, date, licence, page, which seconds). Real people: historical public figures and people in news events may appear; ordinary people's faces are never slowed down or made the close-up subject.
5. Every fact in the voice and on screen goes into `demo/FACTS.md` with its source and the quoted wording; read the catalogue description of each film before using it (it may say what is really happening in the shot).

## 10. Pitfalls

- Catalogue descriptions matter: a picnic film can contain both old-time dances and the Charleston; use only the shots that match the claim.
- Archive transfers start and end with archive slates, "End of Recording" and white flashes; cut inside them. Remove watermarks and archive logos.
- Newspaper pages hold unrelated, sometimes offensive stories next to yours: crop to the fold you need.
- Per-frame auto-levels make footage pump; use one level set per clip.
- `destination-in` irises leave transparent corners that later turn grey under `screen` — paint black behind with `destination-over`.
- Captions that fade before they can be read fail `readcheck`; shorten the words, not the hold.
- A fast announcer outruns Chinese subtitles: 6–12 English words per line, ≤ 23 Chinese characters.
- TTS mispronounces names (Bessie → "Bestie"); rephrase until the speech check passes.
- Old sources are soft: never exceed ~2.5× upscale; prefer wider framings to crops.
- Grain belongs to the mux; don't add it in the page as well.

## 11. Variation space

- **Era**: late silent newsreel (no voice, title cards only) ↔ early sound newsreel (this style) ↔ 1940s wartime newsreel (deeper voice, maps with arrows, march music).
- **Tone**: comic stinger (this demo) ↔ straight reportage (no jokes, still fast) — not for disasters and deaths, where the jaunty grammar is wrong.
- **Material balance**: all-footage, or print-heavy when film is scarce (maps, pages, flip-books carry the motion).
- **Music**: Charleston band, march band, swing orchestra, or a period record carrying a whole section.
- **Packaging**: invent your own ident name and emblem; keep the grammar (searchlights, globe, fanfare, place cards), change the shapes.

Our demo, its story and build: [`DEMO.md`](DEMO.md).
