prompts.text:
# Sports Telestrator — Style Prompt

> The TV football analysis segment: play the clip at full speed, rewind, freeze it, and draw on the broadcast picture — rings under players' feet, marker arrows for the ball, a red patch for the space nobody covered — then play on, switch angles, count the frames, and flatten the pitch into a board. Real match footage is the ground; every line is drawn on top of it and moves with it. A studio show's packaging (sting, corner bug, score bar, a yellow wipe) holds it together. 16:9.
> References (grammar only): touch-screen analysis segments in televised football (the "telestrator" pundit's board), and explainer channels that annotate real match footage. Never copy a broadcaster's or channel's logo, fonts, colours, idents or graphics, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

1. **Watch it, then take it apart.** Every piece of action is seen moving before it is explained. A freeze always follows play; the explanation never comes first.
2. **One freeze, one finding.** Each freeze says one thing (the ball wasn't cleared; nobody stepped out; he struck it from outside the box) with one label and at most two groups of lines. The same few seconds of footage are reused, each pass going one layer deeper.
3. **Drawn on the real picture.** Rings sit under feet, arrows follow the ball's real path, the box line is traced over the real line. Nothing floats in an abstract diagram until the film deliberately flattens the pitch.
4. **Data counted from the footage.** Times come from frame counts (a stopwatch that runs on source frames), distances from the pitch markings (a perspective transform). What the footage can't measure (ball speed, sprint distance) is not stated.
5. **Studio energy.** Bright marker lines, a white flash and a punch on every freeze, the music stopping with the picture.

Not **Visual Investigation** (that is restrained, synchronised multi-camera evidence where the timeline is the protagonist; this is a pundit's show with packaging and enthusiasm). Not a **highlight reel** (no montage of goals to music; each clip is analysed). Not **Data Storytelling** or an infographic: charts are not the film; the top-down board appears once, as a summary, and is reached by flattening the real picture.

## 2. Frame and layout (1920×1080)

- **Full-frame footage** most of the time. The packaging lives in the corners:
  - **Corner bug**, top right (x 1452–1880, y 38–110): show name on a yellow block + a mode line in the mode's colour — LIVE (red dot) / ANALYSIS (yellow) / REPLAY (cyan). It is in every footage frame from frame 1, because it sits over the broadcaster's logo.
  - **Score bar**, bottom right (x 1392–1880, y 926–996): HOME n – n AWAY + minute. The away number flips on the frame the ball crosses the line (a 0.5 s roll with a yellow flash). It sits over the broadcaster's URL.
  - **Source clock**, top left (x 40–370, y 38–90), on every analysis shot: `❚❚ 04.20s F106` — source seconds and frame number; ▶ ½ in slow motion, ◀◀ in a rewind. Hidden in live play.
- **Labels** (black card, coloured left bar, Chinese line + small spaced English line) sit in empty grass or crowd, never over the action they describe.
- **Subtitle bar** bottom, centred at x 880 (its right edge stays left of the score bar), y 938–1044.
- **Split screen**: two 960×1080 vertical windows, each a 960-px-wide slice of a 1920 frame at 1:1 (no extra scaling), a 6 px yellow divider between them, a camera label at each window's top left (A MAIN CAMERA / B HIGH REVERSE). The slices are chosen so the broadcaster's logo and URL fall outside them.
- **Board pages** (shot map, data card): dark board `#0C1411` with a faint 60 px grid; left column text, right side drawing. No headers, no centred title-and-bullets.

## 3. Editing grammar

- **Order inside one piece of action:** live at 1× (original sound) → rewind (0.6 s, reversed with tracking bars and ◀◀) → freeze ① → slow play (0.6–0.85×, frame-blended) → freeze ② → slow play with a stopwatch → freeze ③ → ball flight with a comet trail → another angle (replay), possibly one more freeze.
- **Lighter variants** for secondary pieces of action, so the deep breakdown stays special:
  - **Freeze-in-play**: no rewind; play at 1× up to the decisive pass, freeze, draw, then play on to the goal.
  - **Dual-angle freeze**: both angles play side by side and each arrives at the same instant (each at its own speed) where both freeze together; the same player is ringed in both.
- **Freeze length** 1.8–2.4 s; a freeze longer than ~2.5 s needs a second action inside it. Two to four freezes per piece of action; more than four, split with a replay.
- **Cuts between segments**: only the packaging wipe — a yellow slanted band with dark edges crossing the frame in 0.34 s. Inside a segment, hard cuts. No dissolves, no page turns.
- **Comparison frames** (the shot map, the data card) are fully drawn early and held ≥ 2.5 s before the next cut.

## 4. Colour identity (the one rule that matters)

| Role | Colour |
|---|---|
| The team/player we follow, the ball, main marker lines | `#FFD400` fluorescent yellow |
| Opponents (rings, block arrows, link lines) | `#3FD8FF` cyan |
| Space (a patch nobody covers) | `#FF3B30` red, fill 0.34–0.38 + dashed edge |
| Pitch lines traced, neutral marks, stamps | `#F4F1E8` chalk |
| Show board | `#0C1411` ink green-black |
| Label / bug background | `rgba(8,12,14,0.9)`; opaque `#080C0E` where it covers a logo |

One colour, one identity, throughout the film: a label's left bar takes the colour of what it names. Change the hues if the show needs to, never the three roles.

## 5. Type

- Labels: Noto Sans SC 900, 40 px (30 px for a name), English line Barlow Condensed 600, 21 px, letter-spacing 2 px, in the role colour.
- Packaging numbers (score, minute, stopwatch, big data): Barlow Condensed 800 Italic.
- Clock / frame numbers: IBM Plex Mono 500, 24 px.
- Board pages: title Noto Sans SC 900 60–64 px, rows Noto Sans SC 700 34–42 px with a grey note under each, numbers Barlow Condensed 800 Italic 64–150 px in yellow; text appears left to right with a clip reveal.
- **No handwriting fonts** anywhere: printed type on a dark card belongs to the same packaging; handwriting reads as a school notebook.
- Subtitles: Chinese line (Noto Sans SC 500, 38 px) above an English line (Barlow Condensed 600, 32 px), black bar 0.64 with a 4 px yellow edge; one line per language, never wrapped — shorten the line instead of shrinking it.
- All fonts OFL from Google Fonts, subset to the characters used (`demo/tools/fonts.py`).

## 6. Motion and drawing

- **Freeze entry**: white flash 0.1 s (0.55) + punch 1.035 → 1.0 in 0.35 s (ease-out) + desaturate 42 % + a cool cast + heavier vignette; then a slow 1.2 % creep. Overlays use the same transform as the picture, or they slide off the players.
- **Spotlight**: everything outside a focus ellipse darkens to 0.42 (even-odd hole), 0.3 s fade.
- **Marker line**: dark outline (w + 6, black 0.55) + coloured core with glow 18 + thin white highlight (w × 0.28); drawn along its length; an arrowhead pops in over the last 10 %; deterministic small wobble at the vertices so it feels hand-drawn. Dashed for intended or future paths (a cross, a run), solid for what happened.
- **Ring**: perspective ellipse (ry = 0.36 r) under the feet, drawn clockwise, outer dashed ring rotating at 60 px/s; a vertical light beam while the player moves.
- **Draw order inside a freeze**: ring (who) → area or link (what happened) → label (the one-line finding), 0.3–0.6 s apart.
- **Slow motion**: source frames at 0.6–0.85×, neighbours cross-blended (no stutter).
- **Rewind**: the clip reversed in 0.6 s (ease-in-out), ±13 px horizontal jitter, four white tracking bars, a big ◀◀ and the word REWIND.
- **Trails**: in screen space keep only the last ~0.6 s (ball 0.24 s) — the camera pans, so long trails land in the wrong place.
- **Stamp** (e.g. a VAR decision): a framed card that drops from 1.7× to 1× with overshoot, slightly rotated, with a small flash — once per film.
- **Perspective flatten**: see Native moves 7.

## 7. Grade and image quality

- Footage: `hqdn3d=1.2:1.2:2.5:2.5` → lanczos to 1920×1080 (modern footage at most 1.5×) → `unsharp=5:5:0.55` → `eq=saturation=0.9:contrast=1.04:gamma=0.97` + slightly cool shadows; one grade for every clip; film grain 2 added once at the master (`mux.sh`).
- Broadcaster logos and URLs are covered by the packaging (bug and score bar placed exactly over them, present from frame 1), or kept outside split-screen windows — never by cropping past 1.5×.
- Prefer a broadcaster's native resolution over an "AI-upscaled" stream.

## 8. Sound palette

- **Layers**: English voice-over (one line per freeze, ≈2.5–3 s) → match sound (commentary + crowd at full level in live play; under freezes only a low-passed crowd bed, looped; the goal roar on the goal frame) → score → foley. Voice ducks everything else to 0.55.
- **Score**: sampled band (drum kit, electric bass, staccato trumpet and trombone, timpani, horn, cellos, glockenspiel), about 120 BPM. The groove restarts at the head of each played segment, so cuts don't need a global bar grid. **On a freeze the drums stop**: one brass stab + timpani + low thump + camera shutter, then only closed hi-hat — the music freezes with the picture. Goals: a big brass chord with crash and glockenspiel on the score-bar flip.
- **Foley**: marker squeak (2–5 kHz band-passed noise with flutter) for each line, pops for rings, a tick per landed label, whoosh on every wipe, tape-motor whine on a rewind, a stopwatch tick every 0.2 s, a thump for the stamp, a long whoosh and a timpani roll under the flatten.
- Mix limited before `mux.sh` normalises to −14 LUFS.

## 9. Native moves (and how the code does them)

1. **Freeze and draw** — a freeze segment = one source frame + flash + punch + desaturate + spotlight; overlays drawn by progress (`overlayAnalysis()`, `overlayG1()` in `demo/index.html`).
2. **Tracked ring** — hand keyframes of the feet point in source pixels every ~3–6 frames, linearly interpolated (`TRK`, `at()`); check them with `?dbg=1`, which paints every tracked point in magenta.
3. **Frame-counting stopwatch** — starts at the receiving frame and counts source frames ÷ fps; stops and turns yellow on the strike (`stopwatch()`).
4. **Score-bar flip on the goal frame**, one entry per goal (`GOALS`, `scoreAt()`, `bugScore()`).
5. **Packaging over watermarks** — corner bug and score bar positioned from the logo and URL coordinates, drawn from frame 1 (`bugTop()`, `bugScore()`).
6. **Dual-angle freeze** — two windows, each its own clip and frame range, both reaching their freeze frame on the same beat; overlays drawn in each window's source coordinates (`splitView()`, `overlayG2()`).
7. **Perspective flatten into a shot map** — for each shot, mark 6–8 known pitch points in its own frame (box and six-yard corners, where the penalty arc meets the box line; FIFA dimensions) and fit a ground-plane homography by least squares (`demo/tools/homography.py` reads `tools/pitch.json`, writes `assets/pitch.json`; residuals ≤ 6 px are fine). The strike frame is then drawn as a mesh of triangles in pitch coordinates (1.5 m cells), each vertex moving from its image position to its board position, each triangle affine-mapped (`drawTri()`); the picture fades out as the chalk board takes over, and the other shots' feet points, converted with their own frames' matrices, drop onto the same board (`shotMap()`). The broadcaster's URL is painted out of the source frame first, because the flatten drags it into the middle of the screen.
8. **Data card** — the counted numbers re-stated on a board page: label left, big yellow number right, red marker circle on the key one (`notes()`).
9. **Commentary transcript** — original-language words with timecodes and a translation, in a small box during live play; inaudible words become an ellipsis, never a guess (`transcript()`).

## 10. Material

1. **Ask the user first** whether they have their own footage (club or academy video, their own camera, a licensed broadcast clip), line-ups, event data or photos, and the rights to use them. Their material comes first.
2. **Where to look** (judge every file on its own page):
   - **Wikimedia Commons** (search "goal", the match, the player): many clips are cut from broadcasters' own YouTube uploads under CC BY. Fine: CC0, public domain, CC BY. Not used: CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions", unclear licences.
   - **A broadcaster's or club's own YouTube channel** when its video page says *Creative Commons Attribution license (reuse allowed)*: check that the channel is the rights holder's official, verified channel (not a re-upload or a fan mirror), save the evidence (channel id, verification, licence field, date checked), and download the native resolution, not an AI-upscaled stream. Third-party re-uploads, fan mirrors, colourised or "restored" versions are never used.
   - **Facts** (scores, minutes, how a goal was scored): the league's or broadcaster's own match page or video description, then established newspapers; quote them in `FACTS.md`. When sources disagree, use the official list and leave the disputed detail out.
   - Photos of players: Commons (CC BY / CC0); state the year when the photo isn't from the match.
3. **Before downloading, tell the user** what you will fetch, from where and under which licence. The finder copied into this style, `demo/tools/footage.py` (`search commons|archive|nasa`, `fetch`, `used`, `md`), logs licence, author, page and the seconds used into `SOURCES.jsonl` and writes `SOURCES.md`; `demo/tools/fetch_sources.sh` shows how a verified YouTube CC BY source is fetched with `uvx yt-dlp`. Wikimedia rate-limits bursts (HTTP 429): one request at a time.
4. **People on screen**: players, referees and staff in the event are fine; never slow down or freeze on an identifiable spectator.

## 11. Engine

Canvas 2D, one page: `window.render(t)` is async and deterministic, frames load on demand from JPEG sequences (one folder per clip, 90-frame cache). `timeline.json` (segments with clip and source frame range, voice lines) drives the page, `tools/mix.py` and `tools/cues.py`. `window.TEXTS(t)` reports the text that must be read, for `readcheck.mjs`. `core/render/video.mjs` renders at 30 fps.

## 12. Pitfalls

- **Wrong tracking points** are the biggest risk: reading coordinates off a scaled contact sheet is easily 20–50 px off. Read them on full-resolution crops with a pixel ruler, then check with `?dbg=1`.
- **Overlays not under the punch transform** slide off the players during a freeze.
- **Balls vanish**: long shots are a few pixels with motion blur; colour tracking loses them; frames where the ball is invisible are interpolated and the number says "≈".
- **Numbers the footage can't support** (ball speed, distance run) are not written. Distances only from a homography fitted to visible markings, each shot in its own frame (the camera zooms and pans between shots).
- **Packaging late by one frame** shows the logo: bugs never fade in over footage.
- **Split-screen windows sliding in** reveal what's outside them (a logo, a URL): clip each window to its slice in source coordinates, not only to the screen half.
- **Score state must match the moment**: before the 67th-minute goal it is 3–2, not 3–3.
- **Names in TTS**: spell them phonetically for the voice ("Zayits", "Saduk") and keep the real spelling in subtitles; record the ASR result for proper names in `lines.json` (`asr`).
- **Freeze labels echo the subtitle** and live only ~1 s; anything the viewer must read (scores, board rows, the data card) gets ≥ 2.5 s and goes into `TEXTS`.

## 13. Variation space

The agent decides per film: the sport (football, basketball pick-and-roll with screens drawn as bars, tennis rallies with landing zones, F1 overtakes with racing lines — anything with a wide camera that shows the whole play), the moments, the show's fictional name and colours (keeping the three roles), how many freezes.

- **Three structures:** chronological build-up to the deep breakdown (secondary moments get light treatments, the decisive one the full rewind-and-freeze); one moment taken apart from three angles; a "what went wrong" defensive breakdown ending on the space map.
- **Three openings:** the show sting into a match-record card; the goal frame frozen in the first second, then rewind; the stopwatch running over live play.
- **Three endings:** the top-down board that sums up the moments; the data card with one number circled; the hero shot slowed with the minute and name.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

prompts.text:
# Visual Investigation — Style Prompt

> A cold investigation desk: footage, photographs, documents, sound and maps from one real event, laid out on one shared clock so they check each other. The clock lives inside the picture — timestamps on the evidence, a playhead on a data chart, a stopwatch over the decisive seconds; frozen frames are circled and magnified; quotes are highlighted on the page they come from; a plan shows where cameras stood and where they looked; what is known and what is not are kept apart; at the end every piece of evidence is pulled into one map.
> References (grammar only): newspaper visual-investigation videos, forensic-architecture reconstructions, broadcast verification units. Never copy them, quote their names or use their branding.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

1. **Sources meet at one moment.** The payoff of every section is two or more independent sources (a frame, a photo, a testimony, a report line, a sound) pointing at the same place or the same second. Cut points are sync points.
2. **One clock, read in the picture.** Time is carried by large readouts that belong to the layout: the timestamp on each telegram card, a playhead with its clock on the data chart, a `T+xx.x` stopwatch over the decisive seconds, a frozen "32 s". The scale changes with the story (hours → minutes → seconds → days) at section cuts. A permanent timeline band under every shot is **optional and usually wrong**: it eats the bottom of the frame, adds a layer of small labels and goes empty once the story leaves the clock.
3. **One finding per layout.** Each section says one thing; a heading is part of the layout, never a page header.
4. **Uncertainty is drawn, not apologised for.** `≈`, *inferred*, *schematic*, dashed boxes. Known and unknown are separate columns. A source that does not cover a stretch simply is not on screen yet (it lights up late in its column); never an empty "no footage" box, which reads as a broken render.
5. **Restraint.** Real disasters and real people: no slow motion of the catastrophe, no music that tells you to feel; fire only inside evidence frames; casualties as counted dots and numbers.

Not **Satellite Briefing** (no orbital imagery, no zoom from space). Not **Archive Light Table** (no paper on glass, loupes or hands: documents are flat evidence frames). Not **Halftone Dossier** (no print texture, stamps or collage). Not a newsreel package (no channel bug, ticker or anchor voice). Not a keynote: no centred title slides, no page turns.

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Three kinds of source at least**: moving image (newsreel, CCTV, phone video, launch camera), documents (testimony, memo, telegram/teletype, report page), photographs. Add sound (original commentary, radio, recordings), data (weather, telemetry, counts) and maps whenever they exist.
- **Documents**: a scanned page is shown as a strip or a page, never re-drawn; only the decisive line is highlighted (red, `multiply`, α ≈ 0.6, wiped left to right). Text that exists only as a transcription (a report, radiograms) is re-typeset by code and labelled as a transcription.
- **Archival picture pipeline** (pre-1950 film, max ≈ 2.5×): deinterlace (`bwdif=0`) → crop borders → deblock (`hqdn3d=2:2:3:3`) → lanczos upscale → light unsharp (`5:5:0.5`) → greyscale; one grain for everything. Modern footage: ≤ 1.5×. Never colourised or "restored" copies.
- **One grade** (canvas `ctx.filter`): footage and photos `grayscale(1) contrast(1.22) brightness(0.94)`; paper `grayscale(1) contrast(1.05) brightness(0.86)` (white pages pressed to light grey); maps greyscale, inverted, `brightness(.62)` so they read as dark line drawings.
- **One grain**: six 256² Gaussian tiles rotated per frame, `overlay`, α 0.22 on footage/photos, 0.10 on paper. Grain only on sources, never on type or lines (`mux.sh … 0`).
- **Drawn evidence** (plan, side schematic, charts, dot matrix) is thin line work on the panel colour, marked *schematic* when it is not measured.
- Remove channel bugs, watermarks and the source's own title cards; never generate an image to stand in for a historical one.

## 3. Colour logic

| Use | Value |
|---|---|
| Ground | `#0B0C0E` |
| Panels | `#141619` |
| Hairlines, frames | `#2E3238` |
| Text | `#ECEAE4` |
| Secondary text | `#8B9097` |
| Ticks, *uncertain* | `#4A4F57` |
| **The one accent: here / now / match** | `#FF4A2E` |
| Paper cards (typeset telegrams) | `#E4E0D4` with ink `#1D1D1B` |

Sources are greyscale; red is the only colour and it only ever points: circles, the chart playhead, sync lines, highlights, ✓ badges (a drawn tick in a red box, no words), the zone everything converges on, the *unresolved* column, a strike-through on a wrong claim.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- Chinese headings and findings: Noto Sans SC 700 (30–124 px). Tags, timecodes and ticks: IBM Plex Mono 400/600. Quotes: Source Serif 4 Italic for the original wording, Noto Serif SC 500 for a translation underneath in the secondary colour (only when the subtitles don't already say it). All OFL, subset to the words on screen.
- **Few words per frame.** Each frame keeps only what this beat needs: the main readout or heading, the quoted original (the highlighted line), and one short source tag per piece of evidence. No eyebrow labels, no English twin under every Chinese label, no archive numbers, dates or "estimate / schematic / not to scale" footnotes unless the beat is about them, nothing the subtitle is saying at the same moment.
- **Source tag**: a 6×12 chip + `type · source` in mono, ≤ about 12 characters (`照片 · Pasquarella`, `FBI 电传 · 1937-05-08`), sitting just above its frame. Full credits go on the end card, not on the panels.
- **Lower third**: a red bar + place name (36 px bold) + one mono line (place code).
- **Subtitles** (bilingual films): at the bottom of the frame (Chinese baseline y ≈ 984, English y ≈ 1022): Chinese 34 px bold over English 23 px, centred, 10 px black shadow; **one line per language**, measured in the page against 1,500 px; a long sentence becomes two cues. Original sound gets subtitles too, marked `【原声】` / `[1937 newsreel]`.
- **Reading time**: every key text stays still and whole for CJK ÷ 4.5 + other ÷ 15 + 1.5 s (`readcheck.mjs`); verdict and comparison frames hold ≥ 2.5 s with every item fully in frame. Counters (timecode readouts, the stopwatch) and tick labels are exempt.

## 5. Motion quality

- 30 fps. Elements **cut in** (≤ 0.1 s opacity) with a 3–4-frame white flash, as if pulled from the evidence locker; nothing flies, bounces or scale-pops.
- Only things that are *drawn* are progressive: circles drawn clockwise in 0.5 s (ease-out cubic), leaders and links 0.4–0.8 s, plans stroke by stroke, highlights wiped, typewriter text for telegrams.
- Inside a frame: a slow push (≤ 1.9× on a map, ≤ 1.06× on a photo) is allowed; the "camera" itself never moves. Layouts change on cuts.
- The event clock (chart playhead, stopwatch) eases between keyframes and moves at constant speed inside a timed run (each tick = one real second).
- Scale changes (minutes → seconds → days) happen on section cuts, carried by the readout changing form (clock → `T+` stopwatch → date), not by a zooming band.
- Something changes at least every second; holds are for verdicts only.

## 6. Shot & layout grammar

- 1920×1080, 60 px margins; content y 60–900, subtitles below it (y ≈ 950–1030). Layouts use the full height; no strip is reserved for a timeline. When a section has no subtitle, centre its content vertically.
- Panels are hard-edged rectangles with 1 px frames; footage panels keep the source's aspect.
- Typical layouts: **map → plan** (left) with a reference photo and a footage panel (right); **one big statement + one quote + one wide schematic**; **five-source board** (three evidence frames on top, sound and report below, schematic right, red links converging); **three-column sync grid** (report / photo / video under one stopwatch, each column lighting up when its source begins); **document strip + two-column verdict**; **claim card + fact-check card + dot matrix**; **evidence map** (plan, broken-axis mini timeline, schematic, thumbnails with links).
- Avoid centred layouts, page headers and slide-like page turns. Transitions are hard cuts on a 0.5 s grid, white flashes and the rewind; no dissolves.

## 7. Sound palette

1. **Bed**: low D held by contrabass and cellos; a filtered room tone about 30 dB under the voice.
2. **Clockwork**: a pendulum tick every 0.5 s in the minute-scale sections, louder in the waiting minutes; in a timed run one tick per **event** second (accent every 5) — the audible stopwatch.
3. **Harmony**: a quiet pizzicato ostinato in eighths (Dm – B♭ – Gm – A) under the slow sections; tremolo minor-second clusters for tension; slow sustained chords for the verdict columns; a resolving D minor add9 with vibraphone for the evidence map.
4. **Foley** (procedural): paper for documents, a shutter for photos, Morse "dits" and keystrokes for telegrams, teletype chatter, a rewind sweep, pencil scratches for plans, one deep thump for the moment of impact — then near-silence.
5. **Original sound** (archival commentary, radio, recorded sound): band-passed 180 Hz–5.5 kHz with sparse crackle, shown as a waveform with a red play-line and word-by-word lighting; music ducks −12 dB under it. Original sound and score alternate; never both loud.
6. **Voice**: calm and flat (ours: Kokoro `am_michael`); music ducks about −9 dB under it; −14 LUFS, true peak ≤ −1.2 dB.

## 8. Native moves (and how to code them)

- **Freeze, circle, magnify.** Freeze a frame with a white flash; draw a 2.5 px red circle clockwise; at 60 % a leader and a bold label appear; a ×2 loupe opens beside it, cropped from the same source pixels (never beyond 1 source px per screen px). *Fits:* a licence plate in CCTV; a crack in a weld.
- **Hard sync point.** Pick one instant every source can recognise (impact, flash, a public clock, a gunshot peak) and align each source to it. A source that starts late just appears late; if the gap matters, say it in the voice or a subtitle. *Fits:* which phone started filming first; when the launch camera lost the vehicle.
- **Three-column sync grid.** Document / photo / video side by side under one big stopwatch; each column cuts in (white flash) at the moment its source begins, so the grid fills left to right as the clock runs; freeze on the sync point with a red dashed line across the pictures. *Fits:* two dashcams and a police log.
- **Readouts change scale.** The time readout changes form at each section cut — card timestamps and a chart playhead (minutes), a `T+` stopwatch (seconds), dates (days) — as the story narrows or widens. *Optional:* a bottom timeline band with tracks per source kind, only for a film that stays on one clock throughout; keep it free of labels and drop it when the clock stops. *Fits:* a market crash from the week to the minute.
- **Rewind cold open.** Start on the decisive frozen frame, slam the other sources into a grid, sweep a sync line, then rewind (footage playing backwards, scan lines) to the start. *Fits:* any reconstruction.
- **Telegrams on the clock.** Typeset radiograms / messages land at their timestamps with Morse and keystrokes; red dashed leaders tie each card to a pin at its time on the data chart's axis. *Fits:* chat logs, ATC calls, emails.
- **Data chart with a playhead.** A chart (wind, speed, temperature) across the lower part of the frame with a time axis, event bands (storm, outage) labelled with one word, the message pins, and a red playhead carrying the clock. *Fits:* power-grid load before a blackout.
- **Map → plan.** A real survey map pushes in to the site, then cuts to a measured plan with the subject's position, a bearing, a distance ring, a camera point and an inferred view cone; the map stays as a locator inset. *Fits:* where each witness stood.
- **Evidence → model links.** Every circle in every source sends a red dashed link to the same zone of one schematic; ✓ badges land 0.12 s apart with small mallet notes. *Fits:* which room a fire started in.
- **Then vs. record.** Play a period claim as original sound, then a fact-check card; strike through the wrong words in the claim. *Fits:* a press release against the filed numbers.
- **Known / unresolved.** Two columns, ticked vs. dashed boxes, every item held whole for ≥ 2.5 s, one source tag for the board. *Fits:* any inquiry's conclusion.
- **Dots for people.** One dot per person; the dead become red open rings one by one; a single large number. *Fits:* passengers, workers, victims of any event.
- **Evidence map.** Plan, broken-axis mini timeline, schematic and thumbnails of every source, all links converging; the poster frame. *Fits:* the end of any investigation.

## 9. Pitfalls

- **Inference passed off as fact.** Camera positions, photo times and offsets need `≈ / inferred / unlocated` on screen and in `FACTS.md`.
- **Early reports as facts.** The first-night memo and the period newsreel often disagree with the final report; use them as images or as claims to check, never as the source of a number.
- **Faking a multi-camera event.** With one licensable film, do not borrow clips of unclear origin; cross-check film + photos + documents + sound instead. The structure still holds.
- **Seams in "continuous" shots.** An exposure jump or splice breaks timing; time durations from the official record and state the alignment error.
- **Time zones and clocks.** Old reports may use standard time while the place ran on daylight time; pick one and state it once on screen (`18:25:00 EST` on the first readout).
- **Too much at once.** One layout, one finding; at most five sources on a board, and the subtitle never repeats the heading word for word.
- **Too many words on screen.** Keep only what this beat needs (main readout or heading, the highlighted original, one short tag per source). Eyebrows, English twins of every label, archive numbers, footnotes and translations the subtitle already gives turn the frame into noise.
- **Empty placeholder boxes for missing material.** A grey "no footage" or "waiting for photo" panel looks like a render error. Fill the slot with real material, change the layout, or let the source appear when it starts.
- **A strip reserved at the bottom** (timeline band, caption rail) leaves an empty band when it has nothing to show. Content runs to y ≈ 900; nothing lives in the subtitle area (y ≈ 950–1030).
- **Catastrophe as spectacle.** No slow motion of fire or impact, no full-screen flames, no sound effects on deaths.

## 10. Footage (素材)

1. **Ask the user first.** Before searching: does the user have their own footage, photos, documents, recordings or data (dashcam files, a report PDF, a spreadsheet of readings)? Their own material always comes first.
2. **Where to look, and how to judge the licence.** Use `demo/tools/footage.py` (copy it into the project): `search archive|commons|nasa`, `files`, `fetch` (records licence, author and page into `SOURCES.jsonl`), `used`, `md` (writes `SOURCES.md`).
   - **Internet Archive**: the item's `licenseurl` and collection. The NARA-donated Universal Newsreels (1929–1967) are public domain; other newsreel companies (Hearst, Pathé, Movietone, Paramount) are not, even when uploaders tag them PD. "stock footage" and YouTube-ripped items: skip.
   - **Wikimedia Commons**: read the file page — author, source, licence template. U.S. federal work (Navy, NASA, NARA, NOAA, USGS) = public domain. PD claims resting on "not renewed" agency photos (AP, INS, Wide World): treat as uncertain and skip. Download big files through the API thumbnail URL (3840 px) to avoid 429s.
   - **NASA** (images.nasa.gov): public domain except marked third-party items and logos.
   - **Library of Congress / national archives**: read each item's rights statement; "no known restrictions" is **not** a licence — skip it.
   - **USGS The National Map**: historical topographic maps as PDF (public domain); render the area you need with `pdftoppm -r 300 -x … -y … -W … -H …`.
   - **Government reports and FBI files**: U.S. federal works are public domain; quote them, typeset transcriptions, show scans only as evidence frames.
   - Allowed: public domain, CC0, CC BY (credited in full on the end card). Not allowed: CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions", unclear origin, colourised or restored copies.
3. **Tell the user before downloading**: what (title, length or pages), from where (page URL) and under which licence; keep `raw/` under about 1.5 GB.

## 11. Facts

Keep `FACTS.md` (claim on screen or in the voice → source URL → quoted wording), list every inference separately, and check the final script and subtitles against it before the last render.

## 12. Engine

- One Canvas-2D page (`demo/index.html`), `window.render(t)` deterministic, `window.TEXTS(t)` for `readcheck.mjs` (key texts only; counters exempt), `window.SUBCHECK()` for the one-line subtitle check; all timing in `demo/film.json` (sections, voice starts, original-sound clips, subtitles), shared by the page, the mix (`demo/audio/mix.py`) and the subtitles (`demo/tools/cues.py`).
- Reusable parts in the page: `plate()` (grade + grain + flash), `ring()` (circle + leader label), `cover()` (fill a panel without stretching, returns a source → screen map for circles), `badge()`, `wave()` (waveform with play-line), `playhead()` (event-clock keyframes shared with the mix), `planPanel()`, `schematic()` (16-cell side view with zone/flutter), `push()`.
- Prep: `demo/tools/prep.sh` (ffmpeg + pdftoppm + PIL), `demo/tools/wave.py` (waveform peaks), `demo/tools/fonts.py` (OFL subsets). Checks: `demo/tools/subcheck.mjs`, `demo/tools/final_asr.py` (speech check on the finished film, per line).

## 13. Variation space

The agent decides per film: the event, the sources, the sync point, which time scales the clock passes through, the layouts, the opening and the ending.

- **Three structures:** a cold open on the decisive frame, then rewind and rebuild; one question ("where did it start?") answered source by source; a strict clock (T−10 min → T+1 h) with findings dropping in where they happen.
- **Three sync points:** an impact or flash frame; a sound peak heard in several recordings; a public clock or broadcast time signal.
- **Three endings:** the evidence map; the known/unresolved board left on screen; back to the opening frame, now fully annotated.
- **Other subjects:** a traffic collision (dashcams, CCTV, police report), a protest (phone videos, photos, statements), a disputed call in sport (camera angles, rulebook), a launch failure (tracking cameras, telemetry, accident report).

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

prompts.text:
# Make a style your own

A user makes a style of their own, in one of two ways: **change a library style**, or **start from a blank page**. You plan it with them, one question at a time or in free conversation, prove the look with a style frame and make a short demo film. When they confirm it, you keep it in their own folder in the same shape as a library style. From then on they name it like any library style when they ask for a film. It lives outside the library and never changes it.

Use this guide when the user wants to change a style or make their own ("I want to change this style", "make my own version", "start from scratch", "我想改风格", "做成我自己的风格", "从空白开始"), or when they name a style that is in their own folder. Everything else in a film follows [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) as usual, with the exceptions this guide gives.

Talk to the user in their language. Write the files in English, like the library, with the style's name in both languages.

## Where it lives

Until the user confirms it (§6), a style is a draft in the demo film's project folder. Confirmed styles live in **`~/lemo-my-styles/`**, outside the library, so library updates and uninstalling never touch them. `~/lemo-my-styles/README.md` lists every style, one row each (English and Chinese name, slug, base, one line on what it is, and the folder when it isn't in `~/lemo-my-styles/`): it's how a later session finds a style by name. If the user wants a style kept in another folder, keep it there and still add its row, with the full path, to `~/lemo-my-styles/README.md`.

Each style has its own folder, `~/lemo-my-styles/<slug>/`, shaped like a library style (`MAINTAINING.md` **Add a style**, without the gallery and the release):

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `style.json` | `slug`, `en`, `cn`, `based_on` (the base slug; from a blank page, the technique base), `borrows` (slugs moves were taken from, may be empty), `size` (only when the default isn't 1920×1080, e.g. `"1080x1440"`), `library_version` (`git -C "$LIB" rev-parse --short HEAD`, or the plugin version when `$LIB` isn't a git clone), `created`, `line`, `line_cn` |
| `STYLE.md` | the style's invariants only, in the sections of a library `STYLE.md` (11 in most; a changed style keeps its base's): no story, beat table, durations or end card |
| `CHANGES.md` | one row per decision: section, base, now, why. From a blank page, "base" is the technique base's value, or "—" for something new. This is what the user approves and what you check the demo film against |
| `DEMO.md` | how the demo film was made, like a library `DEMO.md`: it opens with "One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.", then the story, shots, palette, score, build notes and which file draws what. It stands in for the film's `TREATMENT.md`, which isn't kept |
| `demo/` | the demo film's source with a one-command `build.sh` and `CREDITS`: the code and the small assets it needs to rebuild (fonts, data), not renders, frames, `node_modules`, virtual environments or caches |
| `styleframe.jpg` | the approved style frame |
| `styleframe-vs-base.jpg` | changing a library style only: the same frame, base on the left, theirs on the right |
| `test.mp4`, `test.jpg` | the demo film and its poster |

Never write into `styles/` or edit the library's guides for this. The name and slug must not match a library style or a row in `~/lemo-my-styles/README.md`.

## 1. Where to start

- **Change a library style.** The user names one (see **Finding the style** in `AGENTS.md`). If they haven't, do as **Finding the style** does for a film: the full list of library styles in your message, the gallery link, two or three suggestions on top when you know what they'll use it for, then a plain-text question asking them to type the name (not `AskUserQuestion`). One base only. If they want to mix two, take the one whose §1 *Essence* is closest as the base and take only what they want from the other, as changes (list it in `borrows`).
- **Start from a blank page.** The user describes the look in their own words, or brings a picture or a film they like. Choose one library style as the **technique base** (the closest materials and engine: what the code will build on) and at most two to borrow moves from. Make that the first question: your choice and why in one line each, with the next closest as the other options.

Either way, read the base `STYLE.md` in full before the first question. In this flow you may read the base's `DEMO.md` (and, in skill mode, get its source with `setup.sh demo <slug>`) before any treatment: the style frame needs its techniques. The demo film's story must still differ from the base demo's (DIRECTOR.md §11, *Not the demo again*, compared with the base).

## 2. Plan it together

Interview the user until every section of their `STYLE.md` is decided and they know what each choice costs.

**How to ask**

- **One question per message.** Use the `AskUserQuestion` tool: 2–3 options, the one you recommend first and marked (Recommended), each with one line on what it does to the film, and **Free conversation** (in their language) as the last option. Without the tool, a short numbered list with your recommendation, and free conversation as its last line.
- **Free conversation.** When they pick it, stop asking one by one. Post in the chat a checklist: what's decided, and each open item with your recommendation (when changing a library style, also its group from the table below). They answer in their own words, in any order, several at once, or ask you back. When they aren't sure about an item, give two or three concrete directions for it. Update the checklist each round; when everything is decided, or they say "you decide", go to the summary.
- Every question has your recommendation and the reason, drawn from the base `STYLE.md` and what the user said, with concrete examples from this style, not generic words.
- Don't ask what you can look up (the base `STYLE.md`, the library, their files).
- **About ten questions at most**, the technique base included. When more sections are in play, ask related ones together (motion with sound, camera with native moves). If they say "you decide" ("你定", "都按推荐"), take your recommendations for the rest, list them in one message and go on.

**The order** (skip what they've already said):

1. **Use.** What films they'll make with it, for whom, where they'll post them, and so the frame size (a vertical feed needs 1080×1920 or 1080×1440). Their brand or IP: colours, logo, font, a character. They give you the files later.
2. **What changes.**
   - *Change a library style*: first show the three groups as a short message, using this style's own sections and examples. Then ask which parts they want to touch (several may be picked).

     Section numbers below are the usual ones; some styles (Edit & Documentary above all) number or split them differently, so go by the section's subject in the base `STYLE.md`.

     | Group | Sections of `STYLE.md` | What to tell the user |
     |---|---|---|
     | **Safe to change** | §3 colour (the palette within its logic), §4 type, §5 motion (tempo, how much moves), §7 sound palette (instruments, density), §8 native moves (add or swap one) | the style stays itself; give 2–3 ideas for each |
     | **Changes its character** | §2 materials and rendering, the colour logic itself in §3, §6 camera grammar | possible; say what the style loses with each change |
     | **Can't change** | §1 essence (and its "what it is not"), §10 engine | that's a different style, not a version of this one. Say so and suggest a closer base |

     When a safe change narrows a phrase in §1 (three inks become two), adjust that phrase; the essence stays.
   - *From a blank page*: the essence first, one sentence on what it is and one on what it is not. Then the materials.
3. **Section by section**, only the sections in play, in `STYLE.md` order: materials and rendering, colour, type, motion, camera, sound, native moves. Give 2–3 concrete directions for each.
4. **The name**: English, Chinese or both, and the slug.

**Help them change it well.** Most users know the feeling they want, not the section. While you ask:

- Start from the use. The changes follow what the films are for: a weekly brand bulletin needs readable type and a fixed opening, a kids' channel needs bigger shapes and slower reading.
- Turn vague wishes into options, never silent edits:

  | They say | Usually means |
  |---|---|
  | more premium, 高级 | fewer colours, stronger contrast between light and dark, slower motion, more empty space, lighter type |
  | younger, livelier, 活泼 | a brighter accent, cuts on the beat, bouncier easing, more percussion |
  | calmer, 安静 | slower tempo, longer holds, fewer moving things, sparser instruments |
  | like our brand, 像我们品牌 | the brand colour as the accent, not the ground; the brand font for titles; the logo at the open and the end |

- **Brand.** Keep the base's light-and-dark structure so text stays readable, and bring the brand colour in as the accent first. A brand font must cover the film's language (Chinese glyphs for a Chinese film) and allow use in video. Logos and fonts come from the user.
- **A reference.** Name two or three things in it that make it work, map each to a section, and say which ones would touch §1 essence.
- **Keep the signature.** The native move is what makes the style recognisable: swap at most one.
- **Changes that travel together.** Faster motion needs denser sound. A darker palette needs the type contrast checked. A new material brings its own pitfalls into §9.
- **Up to five changes** per round when changing a library style; more are hard to judge. A change the film's language forces (a Chinese font when the base has none) doesn't count.
- **Code draws everything**, as in the library: no image or video generation, which the user may not have. Anything that isn't code (pictures, fonts, stroke or map data, samples) is the user's own or openly licensed, as in TECHNIQUE.md §11, and named in `CREDITS`. A licence the user has to agree to is asked once, and their answer goes into `STYLE.md` so later films don't ask again. If something can't work, say so and offer the closest change code can draw.
- **What doesn't need a style.** Story, structure, opening, ending, cast, sets, pacing and voice (§11 *Variation space*) are free in every film. If that's all they want, they don't need their own style: they say it when they ask for a film.

When the plan is complete, show the user a short summary in their language: each decision, before and after, and what it costs. **Wait for their OK**, then write it down.

## 3. Write it down

Make the demo film's project folder now (`films/<slug>-test/` in a clone, `<slug>-test/` in the user's folder in skill mode) and work only there until §6. The draft style goes in its `style/` folder, with the files of the table above.

- **`STYLE.md`**:
  - *Change a library style*: a full copy of the base `STYLE.md` with the changes written into their sections, so it reads like any style prompt (no "see the base" gaps). Change the title to the new name and add one line under it: `Based on <base name> (<base slug>) from Lemo-Opuscar.`
  - *From a blank page*: all 11 sections written from the plan, with §10 engine from the technique base for now (§5 points it at the style's own code). Under the title: `Made from a blank page; techniques from <base name> (<base slug>) in Lemo-Opuscar.`
  - When the default size isn't 1920×1080, one more line under the title: `Default size: 1080×1440.`
  - Links: the style's own `DEMO.md` and `demo/` (they exist after §5) stay relative; links to the base become `$LIB/styles/<base slug>/…`. Keep every pitfall in §9 that still applies, and add the ones the changes bring.
- **`CHANGES.md`** and **`style.json`** as in the table above.

## 4. Prove the look

Render one style frame with the real drawing code, starting from the base style's techniques (copy code into the project, never edit the library). Check it against the new `STYLE.md` and fix what's off, once.

- *Change a library style*: render the same frame a second time with the base's settings (its colours, materials and type; a stand-in font when the base's has no glyphs for the film's language), and put the two side by side, base on the left, so only the changes differ: `style/styleframe-vs-base.jpg` (`core/render/sheet.py` tiles stills).
- *From a blank page*: there's nothing to compare against. Show the frame on its own, next to the user's reference if they gave one.

Save the frame as `style/styleframe.jpg`. **Show it to the user and wait.** If they want more, update `STYLE.md` and `CHANGES.md` and render again. If it still isn't right after two rounds of their notes, say so and suggest a closer base.

## 5. The demo film (15–30 s)

A short film whose job is to show the style working, not a full production:

- **Topic**: the user's own if they give one; otherwise a simple one with movement and a little light (a kite on a windy beach, the first tram of the morning). Not the base demo's story.
- **Every row of `CHANGES.md` is clearly on screen** at least once, and the native move appears once.
- Music and sound effects, no voice and no subtitles unless the user asks (a voice is a separate test).
- Treatment: one structure is enough (no three candidates). No storyboard. DIRECTOR.md's counts are written for longer films: at this length one real silence and three kinds of camera move are enough.
- **Checks**, as for any film: DIRECTOR.md §11, with its one fix round (no LemoLab sign-off in the film).

Then save it into `style/`:

- the film and its poster as `test.mp4` and `test.jpg`;
- the source as `demo/`, with `CREDITS` and a `build.sh` that runs from there: `LIB=<path>` at the top, library files as `$LIB/…` (never `../..`, also in code copied from the base), and everything it writes going to `${OUT:-<a folder outside demo/>}`. Run it once from the saved folder with `OUT` set to a temporary folder, and check that `demo/` holds the same files afterwards. Code copied from the library keeps its MIT notice in `demo/CREDITS`; that is a licence, not a credit in the film;
- `DEMO.md`;
- From a blank page, point §10 *Engine* in `STYLE.md` at the files in `demo/` that draw the style, then at the technique base.

## 6. Keep it

Show the user the demo film: where it is, and each change with the second where it can be seen. Then ask with `AskUserQuestion`:

1. **Keep it as my style** (Recommended): check that the name and slug are still free, copy `style/` to `~/lemo-my-styles/<slug>/` (or the folder they want), add its row to `~/lemo-my-styles/README.md` (create it if it's missing: a title and a table with one row per style), and tell them where it is and how to use it ("Make a film in my <name> style about…").
2. **One more round**: change what they ask (§7), then ask again.
3. **Not now**: leave it in the project folder. Tell them its path, and that saying "keep the style in <path> as my style" later saves it then.

Only a kept style is theirs: listed when the skill starts, and found by name.

## 7. Revise or use it

- **Not right yet**: change `STYLE.md` and `CHANGES.md`, then render the style frame and the demo film again and replace `demo/` and `DEMO.md`. Change only what the user asks.
- **Using it**: find it through `~/lemo-my-styles/README.md`. Read its `STYLE.md` in place of a library `STYLE.md` and follow the normal workflow in `AGENTS.md`, treatment first, at the style's default size unless the user asks for another. For techniques, read the style's own `DEMO.md` and `demo/` first, then the base's (`$LIB/styles/<based_on>/DEMO.md`). The demo film is one example: never reuse its story, shots or timeline. The films are the user's: no LemoLab credit, no watermark.
- **After a library update**: if the base `STYLE.md` changed since `library_version`, mention it once and offer to bring the useful fixes into their copy. Don't change their style without asking.

guides.title: 3 个提示词技巧:反向提问、先出故事板、喂真实数据
guides.text:
反向提示法(避免翻车神器)不要一上来就让它硬做。 指令范例:“我要做一段[从原子放大到整个银河系]的 10 秒动画。先
不要开始生成,请先列出你需要确认的细节问题,等我回答后再执行下一步。” 让 AI 主动帮你拆解镜头比例、色彩风格与转场
节奏。
先做 Storyboard(节省算力)直接渲染完整视频耗时且吃算力。先给指令:“在正式渲染前,请先绘制并输出各分镜的
Storyboard 故事板”,确认风格方向对了再一键转为动态视频。

guides.title: XML 7 段式提示词框架(xilo 万字长文)
guides.text:
<role>:让 Claude 当什么角色,动效设计师、科普作者还是产品导演
<inputs>:开工前先问你要什么,主题、时长、画幅、配色、参考图、音乐,你没给的不许它自己编
<direction>:画面风格,还有明确的禁止清单
<structure>:分镜和节奏,几个镜头、每个多长、怎么转场、卡在哪一拍
<build>:技术路线,用哪几种代码、怎么渲染、怎么配乐
<gotchas>:这种做法最容易出问题的地方
<start>:第一步先做什么,等你确认了再往下

guides.title: 一个人 + Claude 开“动效视频工作室”(五个部门 + 7 段提示词)
guides.text:
【第二步:搭环境】
工具:Claude Code(当 Agent)+ Remotion(用 React 做视频的框架)+ FFmpeg(检查和处理素材)。先装好 Node.js、Claude
Code、FFmpeg,然后:
npx create-video@latest --yes --blank motion-studio
cd motion-studio
npx remotion skills add
npm run dev
再开一个终端进 motion-studio 目录启动 Claude Code,模型选 Opus 5.5。
目录里放:CLAUDE.md(每次都要遵守的规则)、BRIEF.md(这条片子的简报)、STYLE.md(视觉方向)、STORYBOARD.md(分镜),
public 里放 logo、截图、字体、音频,reviews 里放评审用的帧图和 findings.md,out 里放预览和成片。
【第三步:给 Bot 一本"永久操作手册"(提示词 1)】
让 Claude 创建 CLAUDE.md,核心规则(意译):
- 没有分镜之前不许动手实现
- 只能用你给的真实素材,不许编造界面、数据、好评或产品功能
- 每个动画都由帧号或确定的时间驱动
- 全片只用一种主视觉方向,没有表达目的的东西不要动
- 先渲染几张代表帧,再渲染整条
- 要看渲染出来的结果,不能只看代码
- 问题尽量局部修复,保留全部可编辑源码
禁止项:泛滥的渐变背景、过度弹跳、发光粒子、看不清的字、假的产品看板、没有目的的镜头运动。
一句话:MP4 存在不等于完成,满足简报和验收要求才算完成。
【第四步:让导演写简报(提示词 2)】
告诉它:项目是什么(比如一个效率 App 的发布片)、核心信息(把乱糟糟的项目板变成清晰的冲刺计划)、受众(创始人、产品
团队、开发者)、时长 20 秒、要三个版本(16:9 主版、9:16 竖版、1:1 方版)、必须用你放在 public 里的截图/logo/字体,
不许造假界面。让它检查素材、列出缺什么、写 BRIEF.md、定中心视觉创意、写故事结构、解释每个场景为什么存在。关键一
句:先别写动画代码,等我批准。
【第五步:把参考变成视觉身份(提示词 3)】
让它扮演美术指导,看你放进 references 文件夹的图和视频,提取:字体气质与字重层级、构图与留白、颜色与对比规则、动
效节奏(入场、落定、停留)、质感(颗粒、阴影、边框)。结果存进 STYLE.md。注意写明"不要照抄具体构图、作品和品牌,要
为我们的产品做出自己的方向",先给我看方案再动手。
【第六步:把故事变成可编辑的时间线】
作者的 20 秒示例分五场:问题(0‒3 秒,杂乱的任务板进场)→ 动作(3‒7 秒,光标选中整理功能)→ 转变(7‒11 秒,任
务重新排成清晰优先级)→ 结果(11‒16 秒,整齐的冲刺计划落定,停够时间让人看懂)→ 收尾(16‒20 秒,产品名、logo、
行动号召)。按 30 帧每秒,20 秒就是 600 帧。模型写的是动画代码(用 Remotion 的 spring、interpolate 控制位移和缩
放),不是最终视频。
【第七步:渲染工程师先出"静帧",别直接出整片(提示词 4)】
让它读三份文档,渲染前先确认分辨率、帧率、时长、字体能加载、素材都在,再渲染代表静帧和一小段低成本预览。命令示
例:
mkdir -p out/previews
npx remotion still Launch out/previews/opening.png --frame=30
(再出 action 第 150 帧、result 第 390 帧、closing 第 570 帧)
预览只渲染互动区间:npx remotion render Launch out/previews/interaction.mp4 --frames=90-330 --codec=h264
这里 Launch 是示例里的合成 ID,换成你自己项目的。预览通过之前,不许渲染最终成片。
【第八步:评审必须独立,动画师不能给自己打分(提示词 5)】
最容易被忘的部门。渲染成功只证明文件存在,不证明好看。最好开一个全新上下文,只给原始简报和渲染帧,让它当评审:给
构图、字体、产品可读性、动效质量、节奏、连贯性、品牌一致性各打 1‒10 分,挑出三个最大问题,每个问题写清:帧号或时
间点、看到了什么、为什么影响效果、最小修复方案、哪些必须保留。报告存成 reviews/findings.md。把"让它更专业一点"这
种空话,变成"第 210 帧光标压住了结果标签,把光标提前移走"这种工程任务。静帧看版式缺陷,视频看节奏和转场,两个都要
看。
【第九步:修复循环要有停止规则(提示词 6)】
流程:动画 → 渲染预览 → 评审 → 通过就交付,不通过就按具体问题局部修复 → 再渲染 → 再评审。规则:每个缺陷找最
小改动、保留已批准的决定、只渲染受影响的帧、检查相邻场景的衔接,每个缺陷最多修两轮,两轮还不行就停下说明卡点、请
人拍板;绝不为了过评审而删掉验收要求。
【第十步:一条片子出三个版本,别只裁剪】
同一个故事,横版可以产品和标题并排,竖版要先出标题再让界面铺满。让 Agent 为 16:9、1:1、9:16 分别做版式,每个版本
单独出静帧、单独评审。交付物不只是三个 MP4,还要有海报帧、可编辑源码、素材、联系表和说明。
【第十一步:留下工作室,换项目】
把样式规则、可复用组件、动画方法、评审清单、渲染命令都留下来,下次只换项目内容。评审反复发现"标题消失太快",就
把"必须有阅读停留时间"写进规则,以后每条片子自动继承。第一条片子要搭环境、反复试;第二条可以复用场景架构和质检流
程;第三条还能带上前两条踩过的坑。
【第十二步:存成 Skill(提示词 7)和总提示词】
第一个项目过审后,让 Claude 创建名为 motion-studio 的技能:目的是把批准的创意简报变成专业的代码渲染视频;流程是导
演→美术→动画→渲染→评审→交付;规则是不编造素材、不跳过创意批准关卡、不批准没检查过的输出、修复保持局部、限制
反复修复次数、保存所有重要产物;输出是成片、海报帧、联系表、可编辑源码、素材、评审报告。之后用总提示词开工:填入
产品名、网址、受众、一句话核心信息,七个阶段(导演→美术→动画→渲染→评审→修正→交付)依次走,重大创意决定和发
布前一律停下来等你批准。

guides.title: 提示词只占 10%,90% 靠“挽具”(Lukas Margerie)
guides.text:
【他的完整流程】
1. 先定管线:代码绘制(Canvas/SVG+Playwright)、框架渲染(Remotion、HyperFrames)、混合图像/视频模型,或自动剪辑现
成素材,四选一。
2. 基线测试:在Claude Desktop里用Opus 5.5(高强度思考)对比 Codex+HyperFrames 插件,看哪个出得好。
3. 装"Motion Studio 规则"系统提示:包含渲染约定、视觉禁用项、声音规范、自我批评循环。然后用它测一条15秒的作品集。
4. 做产品发布视频:以创业公司 https://t.co/MzShplMxak 为例,用真实网页截图,让Claude自动抓取素材,写分镜。
5. 配音:在Claude Code里接 Fish Audio 的 MCP,生成旁白、克隆声音。据他说 Fish Audio S2.1 Pro 的API在2026年11月前
免费不限量,支持83种语言。
6. 找参考:从 https://t.co/bKWTVqjMZD 这类站点提取风格指南、帧节奏和视觉语法,存成Markdown。
7. 卡节拍:设120 BPM的节拍网格,用代码合成点击声、嗖嗖声,让转场踩在拍子上。
8. 自我批评循环:渲染接触表,按运动维度1到10打分,多轮自动修补缺陷。
9. 打包成可复用的 Claude Code 技能,当作服务卖。据他说有人做产品发布视频收69美元一条。

guides.title: Claude 不用视频工具也能做视频(Chase AI)
guides.category: 视频框架与程序化成片
guides.text:
第 1 步:懂原理。Claude 用 JavaScript 画布代码生成静态画面,每一帧是时间的函数(他演示 60 帧每秒),再拼成 MP4。
第 2 步:流程是:写代码 → 无头浏览器(Playwright)逐帧渲染 → 检查并修正画面 → FFmpeg 合成 → 加音频。他说除了
模型用量基本免费,不需要第三方视频生成工具。
第 3 步:先出分镜"联系表"(contact sheet),你确认了再整段渲染,避免长时间的返工循环。
第 4 步:提示词里写明四件事:用 Playwright、用 FFmpeg、用联系表自查画面、循环复查直到满意。
第 5 步:给一个参考视频,让 Claude 并排复刻,匹配风格。
第 6 步:用他开源的 Claude Code 技能 animate(GitHub:ch9191/animate),自带剪纸、素描线条、riso、等距、像素、数学
等风格,和"收集需求、故事、风格确认、分镜、制作、交付"六步流程。
他测试 15 秒动效:Opus 5.5 低强度约 20 分钟,高强度约 30 分钟,最强模式要 8 小时。

guides.title: 三条视频 130 万播放的自动化系统(Jay E)
guides.category: 视频框架与程序化成片
guides.text:
【A 创作:3步】
1. 先对齐:用提示词让Claude先问你5个短问题,锁定目标、语气和"完成"的标准,再列出每一拍:说什么、屏幕上放什么。等
你点头再开工,避免白烧token。
2. 给设计系统+先出故事板:没有设计系统就是千篇一律的AI默认风。设计系统是一个文件,定好颜色、字体、风格。他推荐
https://t.co/G9gKLtaWto 找参考。先出几张关键帧静图,改好风格再全量制作。
3. 让Claude开干,像导演一样给反馈。两个选择:
· HyperFrames:HeyGen团队的免费开源工具,Studio也免费,可拖动时间轴自己改。安装提示词:claude plugin
marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes,再 claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes,然后做一条15秒动画开
场。
· 自建"小剪辑台":本地小应用,项目列表,时间轴上点一下打评论,"复制评论"按钮把所有评论合成一条提示词贴回给
Claude。他说用Opus 5.5最好。
· 如果你是Claude Team或Enterprise用戶,现在还有Claude Motion,在Claude里直接做同样的事。

guides.title: 别让 AI 一条提示词出成片,一次只给一个岗位(Duncan Rogoff)
guides.text:
【六个岗位】
1. 研究和写稿:先研究同领域顶级创作者怎么开场,把好开头存进钩子库;写稿时每个事实都对照真实来源,查不到就删这句。
2. 剪:转录每个词的精确时间,只留每句最后一条干净的,其余剪掉;还修正了摄像头和麦克风的同步漂移。
3. 规划:做节拍表,列出每句话对应的画面(有条视频有140拍);先参考https://t.co/AfeGonCaoL等站点的剪辑,完整图形方
案批准后才开建,因为计划便宜,成品贵。
4. 动效:把视频拆成段,每段交给子代理,用HeyGen的免费工具HyperFrames写代码做图形。Opus负责规划和创意指导,更便宜
的Sonnet子代理负责搭建。关掉运动模糊、用半尺寸草稿渲染,渲染速度快约三倍。
5. 检查:从每秒1帧升级到每秒10帧检查,盯6类错误:动画播两遍、图形一闪而过、文字停留太短、图形盖住脸、重复词、口型
漂移。
6. 从笔记学习:每轮意见(一条视频36条)都变成规则手册更新;新意见和旧规则冲突时,改旧规则,不叠新的,他共有12本规
则手册。

guides.title: Opus 5.5 剪口播 + 加动画 + 导回剪映草稿(8 步)
guides.category: 视频框架与程序化成片
guides.text:
1、把原视频导入剪映,什么都不要动,直接点击“智能生成字幕”,然后单独导出 SRT 字幕文件。
2、把原视频和字幕文件放进同一个文件夹,让 Claude 根据字幕进行剪辑。他会处理气口、重复内容,以及自动识别产生的错别
字。
3、接下来,让他根据字幕内容增加辅助讲解动画。
4、他会建议你在哪几处增加动画,由你来决定保留哪些,再让他逐一制作。
5、他还会针对动画的呈现位置给出几种建议,并生成切片图,让你确认动画以画中画形式出现时的具体位置。
6、确定好动画和位置后,再让他根据动画制作音效。他会建议哪些地方需要加入音效,以及分别使用什么音效,比如“咚”“翻
书”等。他会生成对应的音效让你试听,你只需要决定保留还是修改。
7、人物画面缩小之类的都属于基本操作,你可以让他在任意位置缩小人物画面。
8、最后,让他把所有内容导入剪映草稿箱,并将素材放到对应的轨道上,你只负责最后的审核和修改。

guides.title: Claude Motion + Higgsfield MCP 做广告片
guides.text:
第 1 步:在 Claude 里打开 Motion 的 Artifacts,并通过 MCP 连接 Higgsfield(命令行 npm i -g @higgsfield/cli,再安
装技能)。
第 2 步(挑战一):给一条参考广告的链接,让 Claude Code 逐帧复刻:界面动效用代码生成,画面用 AI 视频生成,再让它修
连贯性,并导出成可编辑的 After Effects 工程。
第 3 步:喂三条参考视频,合成一条原创的 20 秒发布片,在 Motion 网页界面里实时改字体排版、场景时长和配色。他说这类
发布片品牌愿意付"几千美元",一个资深动效师要约一周,这次用了 3 小时。
第 4 步:3D 产品片,完全用代码生成;用提示词把卡车换成自行车;导出相机路径、时间和资产到可编辑的 Blender 工程。
第 5 步:复杂动效:粒子、ASCII 特效、多屏界面展示(SaaS 商业片)。
第 6 步(挑战三):做 2D 叙事短片《猫为什么需要护照》,带多镜头角色动画和配音,约 2 小时;用带时间戳的屏幕批注告诉
它哪里要改(比如把文件夹转个方向);只重生成指定镜头可以省积分。
作者的核心建议:目标越具体,结果越能用;需求写得越清楚,模型越不用猜。

guides.title: Claude Motion:一句话出动画(Tristen O'Brien 教程编译)
guides.category: 视频框架与程序化成片
guides.text:
第 1 步:找到入口
打开 Claude 的 Artifacts 工作区,会看到新的"Dashboard"和"Motion"按钮,点 Motion。他用的模型是 Claude Opus 5.5。
第 2 步:写一个详细的提示词
他的示范是:给一家自行车公司做一条 20 秒的剪纸风格动画广告。
写提示词时把这几样说清楚:风格(剪纸风)、总时长(20 秒)、每个镜头讲什么、品牌名和卖点。
提交后能实时看到渲染,逐个镜头预览。
第 3 步:看看它写的代码
点开能看到,Motion 输出的是可编辑的代码(比如 TSX / SVG 动画),不是一段死视频。这一点决定了后面能随便改。
第 4 步:用 Tweaks 面板微调
在 Tweaks 面板里可以直接改画面文字、调整每个镜头的时长和速度。他把品牌名改成了"OBRIEN'S BIKES",把"21 SPEEDS"改
成"100 SPEEDS"。
第 5 步:点哪改哪
用"点选+评论"工具,直接在画面上点一个元素留言。他点了太阳,让 Claude 把整个场景改成夜景,太阳变月亮。
第 6 步:导出
导出窗口可以选:
· 格式:MP4 视频或 GIF
· 分辨率:720p / 1080p
· 帧率:15 / 30 / 60 fps
· 画质设置
(原视频接下来演示了用 MCP 连接器接入第三方 AI 视频平台,把剪纸画面过渡到真实镜头,该段为赞助内容,这里略过。思路
是:Claude 在"自定义 → 连接器"里可以接入外部工具。)
—
谁能用?要不要额外付费?
· 他说目前 Motion 是 beta,只开放给 Claude Team 和 Enterprise 计划,Enterprise 需要管理员开启;Pro 和 Max 暂时还
没有。
· 他说 Motion 本身不额外收费,但生成会消耗套餐额度,按视频时长和复杂度计算。
· 官方说明里,导出的 MP4 还可以交给 Adobe、Descript、HeyGen、Runway 等工具继续剪。
—
没有内测资格?平替方案
他给的办法:用 Claude Code + Remotion 官方插件(remotion-dev/claude-code-plugin),同样是"写代码做视频"的思路,Pro
和 Max 用戶现在就能用。

guides.title: Claude Motion vs 专业设计师实测(kaye.creatives)
guides.category: 视频框架与程序化成片
guides.text:
【准备工作】
1. 在 Claude 里找到 Motion(Beta)功能(视频演示了 Claude Artifacts 里的入口)。
2. 准备自定义技能:视频里用到 Claude_edit_skill.zip 和 paper-collage-film.skill 两个技能文件,另外还有一个 motion
skill.md 和 film skill.md(都是她自己准备的参考提示/技能文件)。
3. 连接 Higgsfield 的 MCP 连接器(视频里展示的地址是 https://t.co/DGGDoCdz54),用来生成素材。
她强调的第一句话:"拿到惊艳画面的人明白,提示词占了 90% 的工作。"
【测试一:给口播视频做动效(约 34 分钟渲染)】
上传四样东西给 Claude Opus 5.5:原始口播视频(Raw video.mp4)、完整讲稿(Full script.pdf)、技能说明 film
skill.md、几张 Instagram 视觉参考图。让它生成带时间轴的动效叠层、字幕和 B-roll。
然后进入 Claude Motion 播放器,看第一版,再用提示词迭代一轮("哪里太快、哪里字太小"这类具体修改),重新播放。导出
面板可以选 MP4 或 GIF、720p 或 1080p、最高 60 帧。最后把 Claude 的版本和设计师朋友的版本并排对比。
【测试二:从零做发布风格的片头(约 20 分钟)】
用 Pinterest 上找的纸拼贴参考图和 Motion skill.md,让 Claude 做一个 10 秒的"纸拼贴"频道片头。先看草稿,再给反馈提
示词,播放最终版,再和设计师在 After Effects 里做的片头并排比较。
【对比表(她最后给的维度)】
成本、耗时、修改方便程度、品牌审美。大意:Claude 在速度和成本上赢很多;人类在品牌品味和"最后那一点人味"上仍有优
势。
【她提醒的坑】
视频里的渲染等待时间是剪辑过的;想要好看的效果,需要外部的参考技能和提示词,不是随便说一句就行。

guides.title: AI 漫剧 7 步 SOP(剧本用 DeepSeek/豆包/Kimi)
guides.category: 视频框架与程序化成片
guides.text:
先有文本,再谈视觉。
工具:豆包 / Kimi / DeepSeek
要点:一集控制在500‒800字,明确钩子、冲突、爽点、结尾钩子。让大模型输出结构化内容(场景、动作、对白、情绪),方便
后面拆分镜。

把文字转成镜头语言。
一集60‒90秒常见12‒14个镜头,每镜3‒6秒。
前3秒必须出冲突/钩子。
工具辅助:剧云、即梦AI、知漫剧等一站式平台可自动拆分镜。
󾠰 角色设定(真正的核心重点)
这是整条流水线成败的分水岭。角色立不住,后面再漂亮的动态也容易变脸。
必须做:角色三视图(正/侧/背)+ 固定特征描述(脸型、眼型、发型、服装、配饰)。
常用锁定方式:
即梦AI的角色参考 / Seedance系列(多模态参考,一致性较强)
可灵AI的主体库(@角色名调用)
进阶:Midjourney --cref、IP-Adapter / LoRA
原则:先锁死角色资产,再批量出图/出视频,而不是每张图都重新抽卡。
Sohu

把分镜变成静态画面。
主流工具:即梦AI(中文友好、角色参考强)、Flux / Midjourney(画质上限高)。
提示词固定结构:主体描述 + 环境 + 风格 + 镜头语言 + 光影。同一角色必须复用同一套特征词 + 参考图。

让静态关键帧动起来。
国内高频选择:即梦AI(图生视频衔接顺、角色一致性好)、可灵AI(动态自然、物理感强)。
技巧:优先用首帧/首尾帧控制,运动幅度宁小勿大,复杂动作单独处理。每段3‒5秒最稳。

声音是第二灵魂。
配音:剪映AI配音(零门槛、直接对齐时间轴)、豆包TTS(情绪更细)。
BGM:Suno或免费素材。
后期:剪映完成字幕、转场、音量闪避(配音出现时自动压低BGM)。

检查角色一致性、口型、节奏、合规标识 → 导出9:16竖屏 → 发布。
